Cost per hire (CPH) measures every dollar your agency spends to successfully place one candidate. It covers internal costs like recruiter salaries and software, and external costs like job board fees and background checks. For staffing agencies, it’s a profitability metric. Every placement has a revenue side and a cost side. Your CPH determines how much of your placement fee or markup actually becomes margin. A staffing agency placing a candidate at a 20% fee on a $70,000 salary earns $14,000. If your CPH for that role was $6,000, your actual operating margin is far thinner than it looks on paper. Segmenting CPH data by role drills down your CPH data further to compare recruitment costs by job. Analyzing your CPH by role allows you to identify which roles require more hiring resources to fill. Returning to our software company example, while the product department has the highest overall CPH, individual roles within that department vary significantly. CPH by recruitment channel = Total expenses for the recruitment channel / Total number of hires sourced from that channel. Drilling down into your CPH data by recruitment channel allows you to compare your recruitment costs across different candidate sourcing channels. [4]: hould I include failed hires in my cost-per-hire calculation? Yes, for strategic planning purposes. If your 12-month retention rate is 80%, then 20% of your hires fail and cost you the full CPH plus a replacement CPH. Your "effective cost-per-productive-hire" = (CPH × (1 + failure rate)) at minimum, plus the additional cost of the failed hire's ramp period and productivity gap during their tenure. Q: How do I calculate the opportunity cost of a sales role open for 60 days? Use the departing or benchmark rep's average daily quota attainment. If a mid-market AE is expected to generate €120,000 ARR per quarter (€1,333/day), 60 days open = €80,000 in missed pipeline creation, not including the slower close timeline of existing pipeline without a rep to advance it. At a 25% close rate, that is €20,000 in lost ARR. Q: Is it cheaper to use an agency or hire an in-house recruiter? Depends on hiring volume. Agency fees (15-25% of base salary) are expensive per hire but have zero fixed cost. An in-house recruiter at €55,000 fully-loaded breaks even when handling 8-12 hires per year at mid-level seniority. For companies hiring fewer than 8 people per year, agency is typically cheaper on a per
[4]: -hire basis. For companies hiring 15+ people per year, in-house typically wins. Q: How should I think about cost-per-hire when comparing different sourcing channels? Calculate channel-specific CPH: take all costs attributable to a channel (ad spend, recruiter time per channel, tool costs) and divide by hires from that channel. LinkedIn typically produces higher CPH but faster TTF for specialized roles. Employee referrals typically produce the lowest CPH and highest retention rate, referral bonus costs are typically 20-30% of a recruiting fee but produce hires who stay 40% longer on average. Q: Does the cost-per-hire calculation change for contract or freelance roles? Yes significantly, there is no ramp cost or onboarding investment for short-term contractors, but agency markups (30-50% over bill rate) replace the recruiter cost. For roles under 6 months, contract is typically 10-25% more expensive on a total-cash basis but 40-60% cheaper on total cost-per-hire basis due to eliminated ramp cost and no retention risk. Calculators of this type consistently organize their input fields around the two categories defined by the ANSI/SHRM standard formula, internal recruitment costs and external recruitment costs, though the granularity and grouping labels vary by vendor.

**A representative example: the ANSI/SHRM-standard calculator**

One calculator built explicitly on the ANSI/SHRM formula groups its fields into four sections [1][7]:

1. **General Settings** — currency (from 15 global options), reporting period (Annual, Semi-Annual, Quarterly, or Monthly, which determines how salary figures are prorated), and Total Hires, which serves as the divisor in the final formula.

2. **Internal Recruitment Costs** — HR/Recruiting Staff Salaries (annual compensation for in-house recruiting personnel, automatically prorated to the selected reporting period), Employee Referral Awards (bonuses paid to employees for successful referrals), Interview Expenses (interviewer time and materials), and Signing Bonuses.

3. **External Recruitment Costs** — Job Board/Advertising Fees (spending on job postings and paid channels), Recruitment Agency Fees, ATS/Technology Costs (subscription and licensing fees for applicant tracking systems), and Background Checks/Drug Testing.

4. **Advanced Options** — Relocation Fees, Candidate Travel Expenses, Job Fairs/Recruiting Events, and Average First-Year Salary, the last of which is optional and only feeds a secondary output (the Recruiting Cost Ratio) rather than the core cost-per-hire number itself [1][7].

The output layer built on these inputs includes the internal-versus-external cost split as a percentage, and, if the first-year salary field is filled in, the Recruiting Cost Ratio, which expresses total recruitment spend as a percentage of first-year compensation [1][7].

**How other vendor tools vary the grouping**

Other calculators follow the same internal/external skeleton but differ in how many line items they expose and where they draw category boundaries:

- A calculator built for staffing agencies keeps the same two-bucket structure but adds staffing-specific internal items such as prorated recruiter/sourcer salaries, ATS/CRM/video-interviewing subscriptions, and training costs for new recruiting staff, alongside the standard external items (job board fees, background checks, assessments, relocation, third-party vendor fees) [2].

- A more elaborate calculator splits inputs into three groups rather than two: **Direct costs** (job ads, agency fees, background checks, assessment tools, candidate travel, and ATS cost attributed to the hire), **Indirect costs** (internal recruiter hours, hiring manager hours, interview panel hours, and days the role sits open, each multiplied by an hourly rate or daily cost), and **Post-hire costs** (onboarding program cost, training during ramp, manager coaching hours, and a productivity-ramp cost tied to months-to-full-productivity) [4].

- A simpler, real-time version asks only for total external costs and total internal costs, recalculates the split as the user types, and surfaces the internal/external ratio "most teams miss" as its main added value beyond the raw number [6].

**Where the grouping connects back to methodology**

In every case reviewed, the calculator's input groupings map directly onto the same internal-cost/external-cost split used in the underlying ANSI/SHRM formula and in general cost-per-hire explainer content, so the tool functions as an interactive front end for that formula rather than a standalone input form with its own separate logic [1][3][6][7]. The calculators built by content-marketing or blog-style sources tend to surround the input form with the fuller methodology, definitions of hard versus soft/hidden costs (hiring manager time, productivity loss during vacancy, administrative overhead, ramp-up cost), and benchmark tables, whereas the bare ANSI/SHRM-formula calculator [1][7] presents the input groups with comparatively less surrounding explanatory content on hidden or indirect costs.

What Is Cost Per Hire and How Do You Calculate It? Cost per hire (CPH) measures the total amount your company spends to fill one open position. SHRM and the American National Standards Institute formalized the CPH formula in 2012 via the ANSI/SHRM 06001.2012 standard, giving teams a shared methodology for comparing against industry hiring benchmarks. Widely adopted since 2012, this formula remains the universal benchmark for comparing CPH across organizations of different sizes, industries, and hiring volumes. Calculating it follows a single formula, standardized by SHRM and the American National Standards Institute in 2012: Cost Per Hire = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) / Total Number of Hires Simple on paper. Yes — there is a recognized formal standard. In 2012, the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) jointly formalized a cost-per-hire methodology as ANSI/SHRM 06001:2012, developed through a voluntary consensus standards development process [6]. One commentator who reviewed the published document independently confirmed it runs to roughly 50 pages, even though the underlying formula it standardizes is a simple quotient: CPH = (External Costs + Internal Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires in a Time Period [7]. The standard defines cost-per-hire itself as "the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires" [3][10].

On terminology, it's worth being precise about what the standard itself calls the two buckets. The ANSI/SHRM standard's own vocabulary is internal costs versus external costs, not "hard costs" versus "soft costs." It "explicitly delineates internal vs. external cost components" [10], describing internal cost factors as "staff, capital, and organizational costs of the recruiting function, including fully loaded recruiting salaries and talent acquisition system costs," and external categories as items like advertising, background checks, campus recruiting, RPO fees, sourcing costs, recruiting technology, agency fees, and travel expenses [3]. The "hard cost / soft cost" framing that appears in the gathered sources comes from practitioner commentary layered on top of that structure — for example, Edie Goldberg, SHRM Foundation chair-elect and co-author of The Inside Gig, estimates that of total hiring spend, "30 percent to 40 percent are hard costs, and the other 60 percent are soft costs," with soft costs described as "the time departmental leaders and managers invest in supporting the HR-specific roles of the hiring process" [1][8]. In practice this hard/soft split tracks closely with the standard's own external/internal split (external, invoiced spend behaving like "hard costs"; internal, time-based effort behaving like "soft costs"), but the sources gathered here do not show the ANSI/SHRM standard itself using "hard" and "soft" as defined terms.

On how soft, non-invoiced costs like recruiter and hiring-manager time get allocated, the standard and the secondary guidance built on it converge on a time-based allocation method rather than a literal invoice:

- **Recruiter time** is allocated by multiplying the recruiter's compensation by the share of their time spent on active recruiting. One worked example: a recruiter earning $80,000 a year who spends 60% of their time recruiting contributes $48,000 to the cost-per-hire pool, which is then divided across that period's hires [2].
- **Hiring manager time** is allocated by multiplying an hourly rate by the hours spent interviewing and reviewing candidates [2][4][10]. Some organizations extend this same hourly-rate-times-hours logic to any interviewer, not just the hiring manager, assigning a monetary value to the hours "team interviewers spend on recruiting" [10].
- **HR admin/coordination time** follows the same hours-times-rate calculation as recruiter and manager time [2].
- Recruiter and interviewer training, while not tied to any single hire, is treated as an internal cost that "can be allocated across hires as part of internal recruiting investment" rather than assigned to one requisition [10].

Two points about data quality bear on this allocation. First, the standard does not require the same precision for these estimated, time-based figures as for invoiced spend: "the SHRM standard calls for high data quality, not a penny-by-penny reconciliation like financial reporting," and guidance built on it explicitly says that where inputs like recruiter salary allocation are estimates, "that's normal," while agency invoices remain exact [3]. Second, because this allocation step depends on organizations actually tracking hours or time-share by role, it's the part of the calculation most often skipped or approximated loosely, which multiple sources cite as the leading reason reported cost-per-hire figures undercount the true cost of hiring [2][4][5][9].

[2]: Introduction Cost-per-hire (CPH) is one of the most important and widely used metrics in talent acquisition. It measures the average cost to recruit and hire a new employee, providing insight into recruiting efficiency and budgeting needs. Organizations track CPH to forecast hiring expenditures and benchmark against industry averages (Recruiting Costs: Budget and Cost per Hire | Recruiting Metrics FAQ). According to recent surveys by the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM), the average cost per hire for U.S. companies is around $4,000–$4,700 (Recruiting Costs: Budget and Cost per Hire | Recruiting Metrics FAQ) (Cost per Hire for U.S. Companies Rises to $4,700, New Survey Shows) (and about £6,125 in the UK, per CIPD data). This metric helps HR assess where recruiting dollars are spent and identify opportunities to improve the hiring process or reduce costs without sacrificing quality. Standard Definition and Formula A universally accepted basic formula for cost-per-hire has emerged: Cost-Per-Hire = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires (in the period) () (Calculating cost-per-hire metrics, demystified | Workable). This f
[2]: ormula was formally standardized in 2012 through a collaboration between SHRM and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) (Calculating cost-per-hire metrics, demystified | Workable). The SHRM/ANSI standard defines CPH as “the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires” (). In other words, it captures all the sourcing, recruiting, and staffing costs incurred to fill positions, averaged per hire (Understanding and Calculating Cost-Per-Hire | JobTarget). Both internal costs (within the organization) and external costs (paid to outside vendors) are included in the total. Most authoritative sources echo this definition. For example, LinkedIn’s recruiting metrics guide defines CPH as the total spend associated with filling an open position (recruiter fees, advertisements, etc.) divided by the number of hires (). In essence, cost-per-hire is a straightforward average: how much money it takes on average to hire one person. [2]: Introduction Cost-per-hire (CPH) is one of the most important and widely used metrics in talent acquisition. It measures the average cost to recruit and hire a new employee, providing insight into recruiting efficiency and budgeting needs. Organizations track CPH to forecast hiring expenditures and benchmark against industry averages (Recruiting Costs: Budget and Cost per Hire | Recruiting Metrics FAQ). According to recent surveys by the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM), the average cost per hire for U.S. companies is around $4,000–$4,700 (Recruiting Costs: Budget and Cost per Hire | Recruiting Metrics FAQ) (Cost per Hire for U.S. Companies Rises to $4,700, New Survey Shows) (and about £6,125 in the UK, per CIPD data). This metric helps HR assess where recruiting dollars are spent and identify opportunities to improve the hiring process or reduce costs without sacrificing quality. Standard Definition and Formula A universally accepted basic formula for cost-per-hire has emerged: Cost-Per-Hire = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires (in the period) () (Calculating cost-per-hire metrics, demystified | Workable). This f
[2]: ormula was formally standardized in 2012 through a collaboration between SHRM and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) (Calculating cost-per-hire metrics, demystified | Workable). The SHRM/ANSI standard defines CPH as “the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires” (). In other words, it captures all the sourcing, recruiting, and staffing costs incurred to fill positions, averaged per hire (Understanding and Calculating Cost-Per-Hire | JobTarget). Both internal costs (within the organization) and external costs (paid to outside vendors) are included in the total. Most authoritative sources echo this definition. For example, LinkedIn’s recruiting metrics guide defines CPH as the total spend associated with filling an open position (recruiter fees, advertisements, etc.) divided by the number of hires (). In essence, cost-per-hire is a straightforward average: how much money it takes on average to hire one person. The ANSI/SHRM cost-per-hire standard, formally designated ANSI/SHRM 06001:2012, is a standardized methodology for calculating the average cost an organization spends to fill an open position [1]. It was developed through a formal collaboration between the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), with SHRM developing the standard and ANSI approving it in 2012 [2] [9]. Under this standard, the metric is officially termed "Cost-per-Hire, Internal" (CPHI), and its formula definition is designed to measure the costs associated with sourcing, recruiting, and staffing a position [1].

The formula itself is simple: Cost-Per-Hire = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires in a given period [2] [3] [9]. In other words, it helps in decision-making around the costs involved in the hiring process and also provides an estimation of the cost of hard-to-fill roles. There are many costs associated with hiring a new employee to fill a role, with some of the obvious and some of them not so straightforward. For example, how do you quantify the marketing material needed to advertise a vacancy? Or how do you calculate the cost of the interview process? The vendor calculators show a consistent pattern: they preserve the internal/external structural split that ANSI/SHRM defines, but they simplify what falls inside each bucket, and the soft-cost and opportunity-cost categories are the ones that get dropped or bolted on as "advanced" extras rather than core fields.

**The structural split survives, but with fewer line items than the standard.** The clearest example is the calculator described in source [7], which is explicitly built on "the ANSI/SHRM standard formula." It keeps Internal Recruitment Costs and External Recruitment Costs as the two top-level buckets, matching the standard's own internal/external division [2][4][5]. But within those buckets it reduces to a small, fixed set of fields: internal costs are computed as "Prorated HR Salaries + Employee Referral Awards + Interview Expenses + Signing Bonuses," and external costs as "Job Board Fees + Agency Fees + ATS Costs + Background Checks + Relocation Fees + Travel Expenses + Event Costs" [7]. That is a compact, closed formula, not the open-ended, itemized list the ANSI/SHRM standard document actually enumerates (which covers separate categories like compliance costs, administrative overhead, training and development, sourcing/database subscriptions, and campus recruiting fees as distinct line items [5]). So the vendor tool keeps the two-bucket architecture but collapses each bucket into a handful of simplified fields, with "advanced options" (relocation, travel, job fair costs, average first-year salary) offered as optional add-ons rather than defaults [7].

**Time-based costs get folded into a lump sum rather than itemized by role.** The ANSI/SHRM standard and most guides separate hiring manager time from recruiter/sourcer time as distinct internal cost lines, alongside recruiter salaries, referral bonuses, and recruiting technology as their own separate items [2][3][5]. In the vendor calculator [7], this is compressed into a single "Interview Expenses" field plus prorated HR/recruiting staff salaries — there is no separate field for hiring manager time distinct from recruiter time, and no line for recruiting technology/ATS cost sitting in the internal bucket (ATS cost shows up as an external-cost line item instead, whereas fuller breakdowns like [3] and [2] treat recruiting software/ATS as an internal cost). This suggests the internal/time-based side is where vendor tools compress the standard's granularity the most, since accurately costing "hours spent" per stakeholder is harder to input than a lump prorated salary figure.

**Soft costs and opportunity costs are the categories dropped entirely, and this is explicitly documented rather than incidental.** Multiple sources describe this as a known, named gap rather than speculation. Source [1] states directly that "most cost per hire calculators only capture what is apparent to the human eye: Job board fees, recruiter salaries, and agency markups," while the "real budget killers... are hiding in plain sight," listing vacancy costs, overtime/temporary coverage costs, opportunity costs from lost revenue during vacancies, administrative overhead beyond what's tracked, failed-hire/mis-hire costs, benefits and payroll setup time, equipment/workspace costs, ramp-up productivity loss, and background-check coordination time as costs that "rarely make it to CPH calculations" [1]. Source [2] echoes this from a different angle, noting that "even the updated figure only captures what shows up on an invoice" and that hidden costs like "recruiter inefficiencies, longer time-to-fill, wasted job board spend, and the productivity lost while a role sits open" are what most teams still miss [2]. Source [4] quantifies the dropped categories most specifically, citing industry research compiled by Truffle that "38 percent of small and mid-size businesses underestimate their hiring costs" precisely because of "expenses that never make it into the ANSI formula" — explicitly naming vacancy costs (~$500/day, with the median 44-day time-to-fill implying roughly $22,000 in unmeasured vacancy cost before any recruiting fee is even paid), bad-hire costs (30% of first-year salary per the U.S. Department of Labor, ballooning to $30,000–$150,000+ per the Toggl Hire 2025 Report once indirect effects are counted), and the opportunity cost of recruiter time spent on administrative tasks rather than higher-value work [4].

**The ANSI/SHRM standard itself acknowledges this limitation rather than treating it as a calculator flaw.** Source [2] notes that "the SHRM/ANSI standard is clear that cost per hire does not fully describe recruiting effectiveness on its own and does not account for factors like time to fill, quality of hire, or hiring manager and candidate satisfaction" — meaning the standard was never designed to capture soft/opportunity costs, and vendor calculators that stick to the formula are being faithful to that scope rather than cutting corners against it [2].

**What this means for connecting a calculator to pillar content:** none of the gathered sources show a calculator UI itself explaining hard-vs-soft cost distinctions, benchmarks, or usage guidance inline — that context appears instead in surrounding article content that frames the calculator (e.g., [2], [4], and [1] all pair a calculator or calculator mention with an extended explainer on hidden costs, benchmarks by role/industry, and how to interpret the number against quality-of-hire). So the pattern across these examples is: the calculator itself outputs a bare CPH figure and sometimes an internal/external split percentage [7], while the pillar-content explanation of hard vs. soft costs, ANSI/SHRM methodology, and "how to use this number" responsibly lives in the surrounding guide, not as an inline feature of the tool.

Across the calculators and guides reviewed, none present their inputs as one undifferentiated total, but few use the literal labels "hard costs" and "soft costs." Instead, nearly all of them organize inputs around the ANSI/SHRM standard's own split of internal versus external recruiting costs [1][3][4][6][8][9], and that split lines up closely with the hard/soft distinction you're describing, even though the vocabulary differs.

**Internal/external as the de facto hard/soft split.** In the ANSI/SHRM framing used by most of these tools, "internal costs" cover recruiter and HR staff salaries, hiring manager interview time, referral bonuses, signing bonuses, and internal recruiting technology [1][3][4][6][8][9], which is essentially the labor-and-time category (your "soft costs"). "External costs" cover job board and advertising fees, agency fees, background checks and drug testing, ATS/technology subscriptions, relocation, candidate travel, and event costs [1][3][4][6][8][9], which is the invoiced, vendor-facing category (your "hard costs"). The Connecteam calculator asks users to enter these as two separate groups explicitly: "Add Internal Costs by entering HR salaries, referral awards, signing bonuses, and interview costs" and then "Include External Costs by entering job board fees, ATS fees, background checks, drug testing, and other external fees" [3][7]. The calculator built on the ANSI/SHRM formula goes further, prorating HR/recruiting salaries by reporting period as an internal line, and separately summing job board fees, agency fees, ATS costs, background checks, relocation, travel, and event costs as external lines, then computing an internal-to-external percentage split as its own output [4][6].

**One tool uses "direct/indirect" language instead, and it doesn't map cleanly.** The Hire Velocity calculator is the one source that uses labels resembling hard/soft costs directly, calling them "Direct Costs" (job advertising, background checks, recruiter fees, onboarding expenses, described as "visible, often tangible... relatively easy to measure and control") and "Indirect Costs" (lost productivity, knowledge gaps left by departing employees, time spent re-engaging candidates, and disruption to teams while positions stay unfilled, described as "hidden costs that can be harder to calculate") [2]. This is a different cut than the internal/external split used elsewhere: Hire Velocity's "indirect" bucket is about opportunity cost and productivity loss rather than staff time spent on recruiting itself, so the vocabulary is not standardized across vendors even where the underlying idea (visible vendor spend vs. harder-to-see costs) is similar.

**One older, simpler tool doesn't categorize at all.** The iCIMS-style basic calculator referenced in one source lists inputs like application volume, staff hours spent on recruiting, HR staff salaries, job posting/agency fees, and new hire volume without presenting them as two labeled cost categories in the interface itself, and it's oriented toward showing potential savings from adopting an ATS rather than a cost breakdown [5]. This is the closest thing among the sources to a lumped, single-purpose tool rather than a categorized CPH breakdown.

**Output: single number plus a breakdown is the norm, not single number alone.** Every calculator with enough detail in the sources produces more than a lone total. The ANSI/SHRM-based calculator outputs the CPH figure itself, then an internal-percentage/external-percentage split, an optional Recruiting Cost Ratio (total recruitment cost as a percentage of average first-year salary), and a worked example table breaking costs down by category and amount (HR salaries, referral bonuses, interview expenses, job board/advertising, ATS fees, background checks, agency fees) [4][6]. Connecteam advertises that clicking "Calculate" produces "a detailed breakdown of your total cost per hire," not just one figure [3][7]. The SimpleTexting calculator "updates as you type" and "shows the external versus internal split most teams miss," in addition to giving "a real number to weigh against what a mis-hire in that seat would actually cost you" [1][9]. Hire Velocity's results page shows a "Cost Per Hire" figure alongside a "Potential Per Hire Savings" estimate and a stated direct/indirect breakdown, though the underlying text is lighter on a granular line-item table than the ANSI/SHRM-based tool [2].

**Benchmarking is attached to most of these, usually via the surrounding content rather than the widget alone.** The SimpleTexting guide frames its calculator inside an article citing SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report ($5,475 average for non-executive roles, $35,879 for executive roles) and explicitly tells readers to compare their number against it, while cautioning that "a cheaper hire isn't automatically a better one," citing CareerBuilder's roughly $17,000 average cost of a bad hire [1][9]. The ANSI/SHRM-based calculator's page cites the older $4,700 SHRM average alongside sector notes (healthcare and technology skew higher, retail and hospitality skew lower) as reference points for interpreting a user's result [4][6]. Hire Velocity's page markets "Benchmarking against industry averages" as one of the calculator's stated benefits [2]. The iCIMS blog, which is more of a methodology article than a bare calculator, goes furthest on this front: it walks through a full worked example (own CPH of $4,625 against a SHRM 2022 mean of $4,700, and roughly $6,500 for technical/communications companies specifically) and then segments cost per hire further by department, role, and recruitment channel, explicitly stating that "analyzing your cost-per-hire data in isolation doesn't provide much insight" and that it needs to be broken down by demographics and data points to identify inefficiencies [8].

**On whether these stand alone or connect to a broader methodology.** Based on the gathered material, none of the calculators function as an isolated, context-free widget. Each one sits inside an article or guide that explains the ANSI/SHRM formula, defines what counts as internal versus external cost, and supplies benchmark figures for comparison [1][2][3][4][6][8][9]. The degree of connection varies: the ANSI/SHRM-based tool and the iCIMS guide tie the calculator most tightly to a documented standard and to segmented analysis, while the older, simpler tool [5] is closer to a standalone lead-generation widget with minimal categorization or benchmarking context. I cannot fully characterize Dora Domosi's "Navigating Recruitment Costs" piece [10], since the gathered excerpt for that source contains only a title and byline with no further content.

message.content:
Across these calculator pages and their surrounding content, none use the exact phrase "hard costs" as a formal category — the internal/external split does that structural work instead — but several draw a closely related second distinction, separating costs that are easy to see and invoice from costs that are real but easy to miss.

**How the hard/hidden line gets drawn**

The clearest explicit version of this appears in the Hire Velocity calculator [2], which labels its two categories "Direct Costs" (job advertising, background checks, recruiter fees, onboarding expenses — visible, tangible, relatively easy to measure and control) and "Indirect Costs" (lost productivity, knowledge gaps left by departing employees, time spent re-engaging candidates, and disruption to teams while a role sits open). It frames indirect costs as harder to calculate but equally impactful, and ties reducing them to refining the recruitment process rather than to a line-item cut.

The High Five/startup-focused piece [5] makes a similar three-way split but names it differently: standard "External Costs" and "Internal Costs" (the SHRM categories), plus a distinct bucket of "Hidden Costs founders typically miss" — the opportunity cost of a hiring manager's diverted attention, productivity loss during the open-role period, integration cost when a hire doesn't ramp as expected, and the cost of restarting the process after a bad hire. This piece goes furthest in arguing that the standard formula structurally undercounts cost for capital-constrained organizations, because it treats a placement fee as a flat expense rather than a draw on a finite, cost-bearing pool of capital.

The most extensive hidden-cost treatment is the "Real Cost of That Perfect Hire" piece [7], which does not use "hard vs. soft" language either but builds an entire argument around a documented gap: SHRM's reported $4,700 average reflects only "direct, trackable costs like job postings, recruiter fees, and agency expenses," while the true figure runs 30–50% higher once hidden costs are counted. It itemizes nine hidden-cost categories that "most cost per hire calculators do not account for": vacancy costs (lost productivity from an empty seat), overtime and temporary coverage, opportunity costs (lost revenue from delayed launches or missed quota), administrative overhead (legal review, compliance documentation, reference checks), failed-hire costs, benefits and payroll setup, equipment and workspace provisioning, lost productivity during ramp-up, and sourcing tool/technology-stack costs. It proposes an "Enhanced CPH Formula" that adds Hidden Costs and Opportunity Costs as explicit terms alongside Internal and External Costs.

The 2026 guide [1] uses "hidden costs" more narrowly, pointing to manager time leakage, tool-stack bloat, no-show interviews, and the productivity hit of an unfilled seat as what standard invoice-based tracking misses, and frames the whole gap between a $3k and a $10k+ cost-per-hire figure as a matter of which inputs get counted, not the formula itself.

By contrast, the more transactional lead-generation calculators — Connecteam [3] and the 2016-era ATS calculator [4] — stick to the internal/external split with no separate hidden-cost category at all; their "internal" bucket (HR salaries, referral awards, signing bonuses, interview costs) and "external" bucket (job board fees, ATS fees, background checks, drug testing) cover only invoiceable or directly attributable line items. The Teamed guide [8] takes a middle position: it keeps the SHRM internal/external structure but explicitly warns that a low cost-per-hire "may indicate... hiring manager time might not be captured, meaning you have hidden costs rather than eliminated costs" — treating hidden costs as an interpretive caution on the number rather than a third input category.

**Guidance on how the resulting number should be used**

Guidance on application varies widely by how commercial the page is. The tool-only pages [3][4][9] mostly stop at "optimize your recruitment budget" and "identify cost-effective hiring channels," without walking through benchmarking or decision-making in depth, though the ANSI/SHRM calculator [9] does add a Recruiting Cost Ratio (total recruitment cost as a percentage of average first-year salary) as a second, budget-relative way to read the figure, and frames comparison against SHRM's ~$4,700 industry benchmark as revealing whether spend is "competitive or signals areas that need attention."

The content-backed guides go further and are explicit that the number should not be read as a standalone or minimized-is-better figure. The 2026 guide [1] states directly that "a lower number can look efficient while hiding poor outcomes" and instructs pairing cost-per-hire with time-to-hire, offer-acceptance rate, and new-hire retention, framing the real question as "is our cost per hire appropriate for the outcomes we are getting?" rather than simply low. It also cites the SHRM/ANSI standard's own caveat that cost-per-hire "does not fully describe recruiting effectiveness on its own" and doesn't capture time-to-fill, quality of hire, or satisfaction — and recommends weighing it explicitly against the cost of a bad hire (roughly $17,000 per CareerBuilder) before treating a cheap process as a good one.

The iCIMS-linked guide [6] lists four uses directly: determining recruiting/HR budgets, optimizing the recruiting process by reallocating spend toward effective channels, serving as a benchmark against both historical performance and SHRM's industry data, and feeding quality-of-hire calculations. It also pushes users past the single aggregate number toward segmentation — cost-per-hire by department, by role, and by recruitment channel — arguing that "analyzing your cost-per-hire data in isolation doesn't provide much insight into ROI"; a company-wide figure can look justified or wasteful only once broken out (its worked example shows a product department with a high CPH that turns out to be justified by technical-talent scarcity and turnover, not inefficiency).

The Teamed guide [8] is the most explicit about correct interpretation and misinterpretation. It states plainly that "cost per hire isn't a vanity metric — it's a diagnostic tool," warns that both an unusually high and an unusually low number carry different risk signals (high often means agency over-reliance, poor job-board ROI, or long time-to-fill; low can mean under-investment in employer brand or uncaptured hiring-manager time), and recommends pairing the metric with a 90-day retention rate or hiring-manager satisfaction score — what it calls "cost per quality hire" — so that cost reduction doesn't quietly increase downstream replacement hiring.

The High Five piece [5] gives the most decision-oriented instruction: it tells readers to use the "true cost of a bad hire" figure, not the base cost-per-hire number, when evaluating hiring strategy, and to divide total cost by successful, retained hires rather than raw placements, treating a hire who leaves within 90 days as zero output against the cost total.

The "Real Cost" piece [7] ties usage to role economics rather than a single benchmark, giving separate cost-per-hire ranges for frontline roles ($1,500–$3,500), white-collar roles ($5,000–$15,000+), high-volume hiring ($1,000–$2,500), niche/executive hires ($15,000–$50,000+), and contingent talent, and argues budgets should be allocated differently by role type rather than measured against one flat average.

Taken together, the pattern across sources [1], [6], [7], and [8] is that a stated methodology — hard/direct costs plus hidden/indirect or opportunity costs, benchmarked by segment and read alongside quality metrics — sits behind the calculator, and the guidance explicitly tells users not to treat the output as a final, standalone number. The purely transactional calculators [3][4][9] present the same internal/external formula but connect it to that broader methodology only thinly, mostly as a lead-in to a product pitch rather than an explanation of hard-versus-soft costs or how to act on the result.

Based on the gathered sources, there is no indication that the ANSI/SHRM standard or the surrounding cost-per-hire literature builds in a matching principle or amortization-style mechanism to align a specific cost with the specific hire it produced. Instead, the standard defines cost per hire as a pooled ratio: sum every internal and external recruiting cost incurred during a fixed reporting period, divide by the total number of hires completed in that same period, and treat the result as the average [9][10]. One CPH guide states this explicitly as a rule to follow rather than a problem to solve: "Keep all three tied to the same time window," referring to internal costs, external costs, and hire count, with no provision for carrying a cost forward or back to the period in which its associated hire actually closes [10].

The one place a timing adjustment appears in the CPH formula is HR/recruiting salary proration, where an annual salary figure is divided by a period divisor (1 for annual, 2 for semi-annual, 4 for quarterly, or 12 for monthly) to fit the chosen reporting window [9]. This is a period-length conversion, not a cost-to-unit matching. It answers "how much of this annual salary belongs in a quarter," not "which specific hire did this recruiter's time produce." A recruiter's fully loaded compensation and a job board's advertising fee are treated as period costs, counted in whichever calendar window they fall into, regardless of whether the requisition they supported actually converts into a filled seat in that same window or a later one [10].

This stands in contrast to how the matching principle and amortization actually work in accounting, per the gathered material. The matching principle requires that an expense be recognized in the same period as the revenue it helped generate, even when cash or billing timing falls elsewhere, such as recording a December bonus as a December expense even though it is paid in January, or deferring inventory cost until the period the related sale occurs rather than the period the inventory was purchased [1][2][3]. Amortization and depreciation apply the same logic to costs that span many periods, spreading an asset's cost over its useful life, or a multi-year contract's cost over the months it covers, so the expense recognized in any given period lines up with the benefit or output that period actually received [1][2][3]. None of the CPH sources describe an equivalent step, such as deferring a recruiter's salary cost into the period a requisition actually closes, or amortizing a long, multi-quarter search across the eventual hire it produces.

The practical effect shows up in how the CPH literature itself flags the metric's blind spots, even without naming them in matching-principle terms. One guide notes that standard CPH tracking misses vacancy costs, the ongoing productivity loss for every day a role sits open, precisely because the ANSI formula only counts costs and hires that fall inside the fixed window, not a cost's downstream effect on a hire that lands in a different window [8]. That same source flags that recruiter time spent sourcing for a role that has not yet closed does not appear anywhere in the official CPH number, describing it as one of several "hidden costs" that "never make it into the ANSI formula," which is consistent with a pooled, period-bound calculation rather than a cost-to-hire matched one [8]. The historical benchmark figures reinforce the same period-bound framing: SHRM's $4,129 average is explicitly tied to fiscal year 2015 data collected in a specific window, and is presented as a snapshot for that period rather than a trailing or amortized figure [10].

So, within the gathered information, CPH practice as codified in ANSI/SHRM 06001.2012 pools all recruiting costs and all hires within a fixed calendar window, and prorates only for period length, without a matching-principle or amortization step that would attribute a given period's spend to the later period in which the resulting hire is actually completed [9][10]. I cannot find, in the material gathered, any explicit discussion in the CPH literature itself of the timing-mismatch problem framed in accounting terms, so any statement that the standard has considered and rejected such an approach would go beyond what these sources support.

The available sources do not contain a formal, independent audit of a specific named calculator (such as hireTruffle) checking its line items against the ANSI/SHRM standard clause by clause. What they do contain is a mix of (a) SHRM's own description of what the standard formally covers and excludes, (b) recruiting-industry commentary — largely from vendors and consultants rather than academic researchers or investigative journalists — that repeatedly flags the same categories of omission across calculators, and (c) one SHRM-affiliated trade-press piece quoting named HR practitioners on the hard-cost/soft-cost split. Taken together, these sources point to a consistent pattern of gaps, but the critique comes mostly from within the HR-content industry itself rather than from outside evaluators auditing specific tools.

On what SHRM says the standard actually covers: the ANSI/SHRM formula is defined narrowly as internal costs (recruiter/HR salaries, hiring manager interview time, referral bonuses, recruiting technology) plus external costs (job boards, agency fees, background checks, advertising, RPO fees, travel) divided by total hires over a consistent measurement period [4][6]. SHRM itself is explicit that this standard "does not fully describe recruiting effectiveness on its own and does not account for factors like time to fill, quality of hire, or hiring manager and candidate satisfaction" [4]. That is a self-acknowledged scope limit from the standard-setter, not a claim that vendor tools have drifted from the standard — SHRM's position is that cost-per-hire was never meant to be a complete picture, and needs to be read alongside separate metrics like time-to-hire, offer acceptance rate, and retention [4].

On what practitioner/vendor commentary flags as commonly missing from calculators in practice: one recurring article (appearing near-identically as two separate sources) argues that "most cost per hire calculators only capture what is apparent to the human eye" — invoiced items like job board fees, recruiter salaries, and agency markups — while omitting vacancy/opportunity costs (lost revenue from unfilled seats), overtime and temporary-coverage "bridge costs," administrative overhead (legal review, I-9 verification, benefits/payroll setup), equipment and workspace costs, failed-hire costs, and sourcing-technology costs (ATS, LinkedIn Recruiter, assessment platforms) [2][9]. The same source states plainly that hidden costs can push the real figure 30–50% above the standard formula's output [2][9]. A separate vendor guide makes a related but distinct critique: it says most cost-per-hire content "defines the formula but fails to provide a Finance-auditable cost inventory that explicitly distinguishes allocatable internal time from invoiceable external spend," which it identifies as the reason mid-market teams can't reproduce their own number consistently quarter over quarter — a critique of implementation rigor rather than formula fidelity [6]. Another source in the same vein says teams "still undercount" the official SHRM figure because they leave out "manager time leakage, tool-stack bloat, no-show interviews, and the productivity hit of an unfilled seat" [4].

On relocation and onboarding specifically: relocation is explicitly named as a category vendor calculators often omit or under-capture [2][6][9], though at least one calculator example in the gathered material does build relocation fees, candidate travel expenses, and job-fair costs into an "Advanced Options" section alongside the core internal/external inputs — suggesting some tools attempt to close that gap rather than ignore it entirely [5]. Onboarding-related costs are treated inconsistently: one source lists onboarding paperwork and administrative processing as commonly omitted from CPH calculations [2][9], while another explicitly excludes post-hire training and "productivity ramp time" from CPH on principle, arguing those belong to a different metric (cost-of-vacancy or total cost per employee) rather than being a gap to fix [6]. Time-to-fill/opportunity costs are the most consistently flagged omission across sources — described as "the blind spot in nearly every cost-per-hire model" [2][9] and as the reason "long time-to-fill inflating recruiter and hiring manager time costs" drives cost per hire higher than the reported average suggests [6].

The closest thing to an independent, named-expert critique in the gathered material is a SHRM Online trade-press article (not itself a calculator vendor) in which Edie Goldberg — SHRM Foundation chair-elect and co-author of The Inside Gig — estimates that of total hiring cost, only 30–40% are "hard costs" and the remaining 60% are "soft costs" such as the time departmental leaders and managers invest in screening, interviewing, and decision-making, which rarely appear in a calculator's line items [7]. Other practitioners quoted in that piece (Ankit Shah of Columbus State Community College, Sharon DeLay of GO-HR) reinforce that lost productivity, disrupted information flows from departing "broker" employees, and the emotional/competitive toll of prolonged searches are real costs that standard CPH tracking does not surface [7].

A genuine limitation of the gathered information: no source here is a scholarly or journalistic study that opens a specific vendor calculator's code or inputs and checks it item-by-item against the ANSI/SHRM published standard document. SHRM does maintain an "HR Q&A" resource titled "What external and internal costs should be included in a cost-per-hire calculation?" [8], which implies SHRM fields exactly this kind of fidelity question from members, but the retrieved content from that page does not include the substantive answer. So while there is a consistent chorus — largely from within the recruiting-tech and consulting industry — that vendor calculators tend to undercapture hiring-manager time, vacancy/opportunity costs, failed-hire costs, and administrative overhead, and treat relocation and onboarding inconsistently, this cannot be characterized as third-party academic or journalistic auditing of the standard's implementation.

SHRM's cost-per-hire figure has moved through several distinct benchmarking cycles, and the calculator vendors in this space consistently anchor their own numbers to whichever SHRM figure is current, rather than generating independent estimates.

**The historical trend.** SHRM's average cost-per-hire was $4,129 in 2019 and rose to nearly $4,700 by the 2022 benchmarking cycle, a 14% increase [8]. That $4,700 figure is the one most widely cited across HR media and vendor content from 2022–2023 [2][6][12][8][11]. SHRM's most recent update, the 2025 Benchmarking Report, revised the non-executive average sharply upward to $5,475, while putting the executive average at $35,879 — a jump of 21% from the 2022 cycle [1][3][5][7]. Several vendor guides explicitly flag that the older $4,700 figure is now outdated and should be replaced with the 2025 numbers when making comparisons [3][5][9]. One source also notes that executive cost-per-hire specifically climbed 113% since 2017, on top of the 21% rise since 2022 [3], and a separate 2024 estimate placed the executive average at $28,329 [8], which is roughly consistent with a steady upward trajectory into the $35,879 figure reported for 2025.

**The executive/non-executive gap.** SHRM's own 2025 announcement highlights that executive hires are, on average, nearly seven times more expensive than nonexecutive hires [1][7], and vendor analyses independently confirm this pattern, citing the $35,879-to-$5,475 gap [3][5]. This split — hard-coded into SHRM's benchmarking methodology as separate "Nonexecutive Average" and "Executive Average" line items [1][7] — is the single most consistently cited driver of cost-per-hire variation across sources.

**Other cited drivers of variation:**

- **Role seniority**, treated as a finer-grained version of the executive/non-executive split. One vendor synthesis (citing SHRM and ScoutLogic data) breaks this into a spectrum: entry-level at $2,000–$3,000, mid-level professional at $4,000–$6,000, technical/engineering at $6,200–$8,000, senior/director at $10,000–$20,000, and executive (C-suite) at $28,000–$35,879 — a roughly 12x gap between entry-level and executive hiring, attributed to differences in sourcing complexity, competitive offers, search-cycle length, and reliance on retained search firms and relocation packages [3].

- **Industry**, cited by SHRM's 2025 reports as one of the segmentation dimensions in its 88 individual data sets [1][7], and elaborated by vendor data (citing TimeClick's analysis) showing retail/hospitality at $2,700, technology at $6,200–$8,000, healthcare at $9,000–$12,000, skilled trades at $12,000+, and legal/professional services at $16,000–$20,000, with healthcare singled out as running two to three times the national average due to credential verification, licensing requirements, and talent shortages [3].

- **Company size**, cited by SHRM as one of its benchmarking segmentations [1][7] and discussed at length by vendor sources: smaller companies often show higher per-hire costs despite lower total spending because they lack dedicated recruiting teams and scale, and rely more heavily on agencies or job boards, while larger organizations spread fixed costs (ATS licenses, recruiter salaries, employer branding) across many more hires [3][5]. One survey found cost-per-hire is the top-tracked HR metric for 47% of businesses with 5–19 employees and 54% of businesses with 20–49 employees [3][5].

- **Geography/region**, cited by SHRM's 2025 reports as a segmentation dimension alongside industry, sector, and organization size [1][7], and discussed independently by another source, which notes that North America and Europe typically carry higher salary expectations, benefits costs, and recruitment fees than emerging markets such as India, Vietnam, or the Philippines, though logistical and compliance costs can offset some of that difference [11].

- **Process maturity / manual vs. automated workflows.** Multiple vendor sources argue that whether an organization still relies on manual screening versus AI-assisted tools is itself a driver of variation, citing AI adopters reporting cost-per-hire reductions of 30% or more [3][5].

**The hard-cost/soft-cost framing.** Separately from these segmentation factors, several sources (built around the same SHRM-affiliated commentary from Edie Goldberg) frame cost-per-hire variation through a hard-cost/soft-cost lens rather than a demographic one: roughly 30–40% of total recruiting cost is "hard cost" (the SHRM-measured direct spend, historically around $4,700), while the remaining 60% is "soft cost" — time invested by hiring managers and departmental leaders in screening, interviewing, and decision-making — which can multiply the true cost of hiring by 2x to 3x beyond the quoted average [2][6][12][8]. This soft-cost/hard-cost distinction is presented as a separate axis of variation from the industry/seniority/size/geography breakdown SHRM's benchmarking segments cover.

[3]: Introduction Cost-per-hire (CPH) is one of the most important and widely used metrics in talent acquisition. It measures the average cost to recruit and hire a new employee, providing insight into recruiting efficiency and budgeting needs. Organizations track CPH to forecast hiring expenditures and benchmark against industry averages (Recruiting Costs: Budget and Cost per Hire | Recruiting Metrics FAQ). According to recent surveys by the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM), the average cost per hire for U.S. companies is around $4,000–$4,700 (Recruiting Costs: Budget and Cost per Hire | Recruiting Metrics FAQ) (Cost per Hire for U.S. Companies Rises to $4,700, New Survey Shows) (and about £6,125 in the UK, per CIPD data). This metric helps HR assess where recruiting dollars are spent and identify opportunities to improve the hiring process or reduce costs without sacrificing quality. Standard Definition and Formula A universally accepted basic formula for cost-per-hire has emerged: Cost-Per-Hire = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires (in the period) () (Calculating cost-per-hire metrics, demystified | Workable). This f
[3]: ormula was formally standardized in 2012 through a collaboration between SHRM and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) (Calculating cost-per-hire metrics, demystified | Workable). The SHRM/ANSI standard defines CPH as “the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires” (). In other words, it captures all the sourcing, recruiting, and staffing costs incurred to fill positions, averaged per hire (Understanding and Calculating Cost-Per-Hire | JobTarget). Both internal costs (within the organization) and external costs (paid to outside vendors) are included in the total. Most authoritative sources echo this definition. For example, LinkedIn’s recruiting metrics guide defines CPH as the total spend associated with filling an open position (recruiter fees, advertisements, etc.) divided by the number of hires (). In essence, cost-per-hire is a straightforward average: how much money it takes on average to hire one person. Based on the gathered information, the ANSI/SHRM standard and the broader CPH literature do not frame the hire-event cutoff using COGS/TCO-style accounting-boundary language, and no single commonly used "total cost of a hire" metric parallel to TCO appears in the sources. What the literature does show is a consistent, but differently articulated, cutoff and a scatter of separate downstream metrics rather than one extended metric.

**The cutoff itself is treated as definitional, not argued as a deliberate boundary choice.** The SHRM/ANSI 06001:2012 standard defines cost-per-hire simply as "the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires," covering sourcing, recruiting, and staffing costs [3][10]. Sources describe this cutoff functionally rather than theoretically: CPH covers "all recruitment costs to get an employee to day 1" and explicitly excludes "the new employee's salary, training after hire, or lost productivity during ramp-up" [3][10]. Another source states plainly that CPH "doesn't include post-hire costs like training beyond initial onboarding, productivity ramp time, or ongoing employment costs" [9]. None of the gathered sources characterize this exclusion as an intentional accounting-boundary decision analogous to how COGS stops at the point of production — the literature simply states what is and isn't in scope, without the kind of accounting-theory justification your question is asking about.

**The literature does clearly distinguish CPH from post-hire costs, but assigns those costs to separate, unnamed-as-a-unified-standard metrics rather than one extended "TCO of a hire" metric.** One source is explicit that onboarding cost and cost-per-hire are "two different metrics with different timing and components," calling them "sequential costs with different timelines" where "solving one does not solve the other" [4]. That source reports SHRM's cost-per-hire average ($4,700) alongside a separate SHRM onboarding-cost average ($4,100), treating them as adjacent but distinct figures rather than components of one combined metric [4]. Similarly, a source aimed at mid-market recruiting teams states that post-hire costs "belong to different metrics like cost-of-vacancy and time-to-productivity" [9], and elsewhere that they belong "to separate metrics like total cost per employee," warning that "mixing recruiting costs with onboarding costs makes your CPH impossible to benchmark against industry standards" [9]. This suggests the field actively resists folding onboarding/ramp-up costs into CPH, specifically to preserve benchmarking comparability — the opposite instinct from a TCO framing, which deliberately extends the boundary.

**No single named extended metric analogous to TCO emerges from the sources.** Instead, several partial, non-unified metrics appear scattered across the literature: "cost-of-vacancy" and "time-to-productivity" as separate tracked figures [8][9]; "total cost per employee" as a catch-all label for ongoing employment cost [9]; "quality-of-hire" and "cost-per-quality-hire," which some sources argue should be paired with CPH so organizations aren't "optimising for cheap hires that don't stick" [5][9]; and the Recruiting Cost Ratio (RCR), described as "a ratio of costs to total first-year annual compensation of the new hires," which is a different SHRM-related standard but is a ratio, not a cost-forward-carrying total [6]. One source also computes what a fully loaded number could look like informally — noting that "a single $75,000 role can cost over $62,000 to fill" once vacancy costs and bad-hire risk are factored in — but this is presented as an ad hoc illustrative calculation, not a codified or commonly used named metric [8]. Bad-hire cost (up to 30% of first-year salary, per the U.S. Department of Labor, with indirect costs ballooning to $30,000–$150,000+) is likewise tracked as its own distinct figure rather than folded into an extended CPH [8].

In short, the gathered information indicates that the CPH literature draws a real practical line at the hire event — largely to protect benchmarking consistency — but it does not narrate that line as a deliberate accounting-philosophy choice the way COGS-versus-TCO is normally framed, and it does not converge on one commonly used "total cost of a hire" successor metric. Instead it disperses ramp-up, onboarding, vacancy, and bad-hire costs across several separately named, individually tracked metrics (onboarding cost, cost-of-vacancy, time-to-productivity, bad-hire cost, total cost per employee, cost-per-quality-hire), which several sources explicitly recommend using alongside CPH rather than merging into it [4][8][9].

What Is Cost Per Hire and How Do You Calculate It? Cost per hire (CPH) measures the total amount your company spends to fill one open position. Existing cost-per-hire calculators overwhelmingly present themselves as implementations of the ANSI/SHRM standard rather than as unaffiliated, purely proprietary tools. The calculator excerpts in the gathered information (sources [1] and [8], which appear to describe the same tool, likely hireTruffle's own calculator) state explicitly and repeatedly that the tool "accurately calculate[s] your cost-per-hire using the ANSI/SHRM standard formula" and that it is "based on the ANSI/SHRM standard formula" [1][8]. The calculator's FAQ section reinforces this by answering "How do you calculate cost per hire?" with "Cost per hire is calculated using the ANSI/SHRM standard formula" [1][8]. So rather than isolating itself as a standalone widget, this calculator explicitly frames every line item — HR/recruiting salaries, referral awards, interview expenses, signing bonuses, job board fees, agency fees, ATS costs, background checks, relocation, and travel — as a subcomponent of the recognized ANSI/SHRM formula, and it layers on pillar-content style explanation of internal versus external costs, benchmarking, and how to use the resulting number for budget optimization, forecasting, and workforce planning [1][8].

This pattern holds across the other vendor and consultancy content gathered. Teamed's guide states the formula is "SHRM-standard" and frames its entire walkthrough — definitions of internal versus external costs, a step-by-step calculation process, and benchmark tables — around that standard, while also noting that "most cost-per-hire content defines the formula but fails to provide a Finance-auditable cost inventory," implying that many competing calculators cite the standard nominally without operationalizing it fully [3]. A recruiting-technology guide (source [7]) explicitly credits "SHRM and the American National Standards Institute" for formalizing the CPH formula "in 2012 via the ANSI/SHRM 06001.2012 standard," describing it as "the universal benchmark for comparing CPH across organizations," and structures its own benchmarks and hidden-cost discussion as an elaboration on that standardized base rather than a competing proprietary formula [7]. Notably, this same source cites "industry research compiled by Truffle" as a data point on underestimated hiring costs, indicating that Truffle (hireTruffle) is treated by at least one other vendor as a source tied to the standard CPH conversation rather than a disconnected competitor with its own methodology [7].

Another guide (source [10]) is explicit that "the widely used version comes from the ANSI/SHRM 06001.2012 standard" and structures its entire explanation — external costs, internal costs, a worked example, common mistakes, and even what the standard deliberately excludes (post-hire salary, onboarding, ramp-up productivity loss, vacancy cost) — around that named standard, treating the standard itself as the pillar reference point for every line item discussed [10]. A commentary source (source [9]) independently confirms the standard's existence and formal weight, noting sardonically that "an American National Standard for calculating the Cost Per Hire has been published" as "a 50 page American National Standard" reducible to CPH = (External Costs + Internal Costs) / Total Number of Hires, and links to "ANSI/SHRM 06001.2012" directly [9]. A separate technical reference (source [4]) confirms the standard specifies "a more restrictive set" of cost categories for a comparable ("CPHC") version of the formula, and source [6] confirms ANSI standards generally distinguish mandatory ("shall") requirements from recommendations, which is relevant to how strictly a vendor calculator can claim compliance with the named standard [4][6]. SHRM's own resource pages likewise host Q&A content on "what external and internal costs should be included in a cost-per-hire calculation," positioning SHRM as the standard-setting body vendors reference back to [2].

At the same time, the gathered information shows that not every vendor's presentation stops at the bare ANSI/SHRM formula — several explicitly critique it as insufficient on its own and layer proprietary "enhanced" or "hidden cost" framings on top of it while still citing it as the base. One source states that "the cost per hire formula, as defined by the American Standards Institute (ANSI) and the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM)... offers a useful starting point" but argues its "scope still is limited," then proposes an "Enhanced CPH Formula" that adds hidden costs and opportunity costs to the ANSI/SHRM base rather than replacing it [5]. This indicates that even vendors building more elaborate, proprietary-flavored calculators tend to anchor their methodology explicitly to the named ANSI/SHRM standard first, then extend it, rather than presenting an unreferenced, free-floating formula.

Taken together, the gathered information does not show any calculator presenting a formula that omits reference to the ANSI/SHRM standard entirely. Every vendor or informational source in this set that shows or describes a formula — the calculator itself, Teamed, the AI-recruiting guide, the Codeless/CPH guide, and even a critical blog commentary — names ANSI/SHRM (or "SHRM-standard") explicitly and ties its internal/external cost breakdown, benchmarks, and usage guidance back to that named standard, sometimes while also noting the standard's limitations (its exclusion of vacancy costs, bad-hire costs, and post-hire productivity loss) as the basis for proprietary "hidden cost" extensions [1][3][5][7][8][9][10]. I cannot confirm from the gathered information whether hireTruffle's calculator differs from source [1]/[8] in its exact framing, since the excerpts describing "hireTruffle" by name only appear as a citation for a hidden-cost statistic in source [7], not as the direct source of a calculator's own formula page; the calculator content in [1] and [8] is unattributed to a specific named vendor in the excerpts provided.

Knowing what it will cost you to source new talent can help you figure out where you should either cut costs (as is so often desired by your CFO), or where you’re able to invest more for high quality hires. Finding the right balance can cause headaches, so we’re here to help you make those data driven decisions. What is “cost per hire?” Simply put, “cost per hire” is the amount of budget that you spend on making a hire. If you’re wondering what that number might look like, the average CPH was $4,129 in a recent survey from Society of Human Resource Management (SHRM). This number will of course vary depending on your hiring needs, but it’s important to note that this metric is crucial to track when you’re putting together your recruiting budget. The importance of measuring cost per hire There are many factors to consider in the recruitment process, but CPH is essentially the most important metric for talent analytics. They only know what they can see on the invoice.â That stuck with me, because he was right. Youâve probably seen the $4,700 average cost per hire figure floating around. That number is out of date, and current SHRM benchmarks put the real figure noticeably higher (more on that below). Even the updated figure only captures what shows up on an invoice. What most teams still
[6]: miss are the hidden costs pushing the real total higher: recruiter inefficiencies, longer time-to-fill, wasted job board spend, and the productivity lost while a role sits open. If you want your own number before you keep reading, the free calculator further down does the math in under a minute. Even in a softer labor market, hiring hasnât gotten cheap. Wage pressure, turnover, and fragmented workflows are still keeping costs stubbornly high. If you havenât recalculated your true cost per hire recently, now is the time. This article will show you how. What is cost per hire? Cost per hire is a recruiting metric that measures the average total expense required to hire a new employee. In the SHRM/ANSI standard, itâs defined as the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires, using internal and external recruiting costs gathered over the same measurement period. That includes the obvious costs, like job ads and agency fees, and the less visible ones, like recruiter time, hiring manager time, and recruiting technology. This metric matters because recruiting rarely gets expensive in one dramatic place. Costs usually spread out across sourcing, screening, coordination, and
[6]: vendor spend. Cost per hire gives you one number that helps make that sprawl visible. Why cost per hire matters for recruiting teams Tracking cost per hire helps recruiting teams understand whether the hiring process is efficient, where money is being wasted, and how hiring costs change by role, team, or business unit. It is especially useful for: - Budget planning - Process optimization - Channel comparison - Stakeholder reporting Used well, cost per hire tells you whether youâre overspending on agencies for certain roles, whether hiring managers are burning too much time in early-stage interviews, and whether costs are rising because the process is slow rather than because talent got more expensive. The SHRM standard also notes that cost-per-hire has long been used to support budgeting and benchmark recruiting effectiveness and staffing efficiency. The cost per hire formula The standard formula is: (Internal Costs + External Costs) / Total Number of Hires = Cost Per Hire The key is consistency. Your costs and your hires need to be measured across the same period, whether thatâs monthly, quarterly, or annually. Internal recruiting costs Internal costs are the expenses tied to your
[6]: in-house recruiting effort. These often include: - Recruiter salaries and benefits - Hiring manager time spent reviewing candidates and interviewing - Recruiting technology such as your ATS, video interview platform, and assessment tools - Employee referral bonuses - Internal training for recruiters or interviewers The SHRM/ANSI standard describes internal cost factors as staff, capital, and organizational costs of the recruiting function, including fully loaded recruiting salaries and talent acquisition system costs. External recruiting costs External costs are payments made to outside vendors or services. These often include: - Job board fees - Recruitment agency fees - Background checks and drug screenings - Employer branding spend tied to recruiting - Career fairs and recruiting events - Candidate travel or reimbursed expenses The same standard includes external categories such as advertising, background checks, campus recruiting, RPO fees, sourcing costs, recruiting technology, agency fees, and travel expenses. Total number of hires This is the number of employees who accepted offers and started during the measurement period. If you calculate costs over a quarter, use the hir
[6]: es from that same quarter. Donât compare annual costs against monthly or quarterly hires, and count whole hires rather than fractional full-time-equivalents. External costs come to $6,000: job board posts, a couple of background checks, and one contingency agency fee. Internal costs come to $9,000, mostly hiring manager and recruiter time spent reviewing resumes, interviewing, and coordinating. ($6,000 + $9,000) Ã· 8 hires = $1,875 per hire. Thatâs well below the SHRM average, and it should be. A 40-person company isnât filling executive or specialized technical roles at the same rate as a large enterprise. The point isnât to hit a benchmark. Itâs to know your own number well enough to notice when it moves. [6]: tems - Vendor invoices - Recruiting software subscriptions - Internal time estimates for recruiters and hiring managers Some inputs will be exact, like agency invoices. Others will be estimates, like recruiter salary allocation. Thatâs normal. The SHRM standard calls for high data quality, not a penny-by-penny reconciliation like financial reporting. 2. Add up internal costs Now total your internal recruiting costs. This usually includes: - The portion of recruiter salaries and benefits tied to hiring - Hiring manager interview and review time - Internal recruiting software and infrastructure - Referral bonuses - Training or enablement costs connected to the hiring process The hardest part is usually salary allocation. If recruiters split time across hiring, operations, and employer branding, use a reasonable hours-based estimate for the hiring-related portion rather than leaving it out completely. 3. Add up external costs Next, total your external costs. These usually include: - Job board invoices - Agency fees - Background check bills - Assessment vendor costs - Event and career fair spend - Candidate travel reimbursements This is usually the easier half, since the data lives in
[6]: invoices and contracts. Include both fixed costs, like annual subscriptions, and variable costs, like per-hire or per-candidate fees. 4. Divide by total hires Once you have total internal costs and total external costs, divide the combined number by total hires in the same period, the same way we did in the example above. That gives you your average cost per hire, both company-wide and, more usefully, segmented by department, role family, or location (more on why that split matters below). [6]: e cited in a lot of places. Your own cost per hire will vary by industry, role level, and how much of the process still runs on manual screening versus tools that automate part of it. Paychexâs 2026 Business Leaders Priorities survey found cost per hire is the #1 HR metric tracked by 47% of businesses with 5 to 19 employees, and 54% of businesses with 20 to 49 employees. If you obsess over this number, youâre not overthinking it. Youâre in the majority. What is a good cost per hire for your company A good cost per hire is not simply a low one. A lower number can look efficient while hiding poor outcomes. If those hires leave quickly, underperform, or require the process to restart, your true hiring cost is much higher than the metric suggests. Thatâs why cost per hire should be tracked alongside: - Time to hire - Offer acceptance rate - New hire retention
[6]: - Quality of hire The SHRM/ANSI standard is clear that cost per hire does not fully describe recruiting effectiveness on its own and does not account for factors like time to fill, quality of hire, or hiring manager and candidate satisfaction. CareerBuilder research puts the average cost of a bad hire around $17,000, once you count wasted salary, lost productivity, retraining, and starting the search over. Thatâs a broad industry estimate, not a precise number for your business, but it makes the point on its own: one bad hire usually costs more than the entire process that produced it. Thatâs why cost per hire and quality of hire have to be read together, not traded off. At a small business, it usually measures the ownerâs evening, after the actual

Thatâs part of why cost per hire is the top HR metric for nearly half of businesses under 20 people in the Paychex survey above. It isnât an abstract KPI. Itâs the number that tells you whether hiring is quietly eating your week. The upside is that small teams have the most to gain from fixing this. Remove a few hours of manual screening or scheduling from each role and the impact shows up fast, because those hours were coming out of your own schedule, not a specialistâs.
