Across the vendor tools represented in the gathered material, none simply return a bare number with no interpretive framing. Every calculator or calculator-adjacent guide pairs the ANSI/SHRM output with at least a stated industry-average figure, and most go further with segmented breakdowns by role, industry, or company size, plus explicit warnings that a low number is not automatically a "good" one.

The clearest case of benchmark data displayed directly alongside a calculator is the tool described in [4]. Its own explanatory text states: "Industry benchmarks provide essential context for evaluating your own CPH results. According to SHRM data, the average cost per hire across all industries is approximately $4,700, while executive and C-suite positions routinely exceed $14,000 per hire." It further breaks that average down qualitatively by sector, noting that "Healthcare and technology sectors, where specialized skills are in high demand, tend to report higher-than-average recruitment costs, whereas retail and hospitality roles with higher volume and lower specialization fall below the median," and closes with "Comparing your calculated cost-per-hire against these benchmarks reveals whether your recruitment spending is competitive or signals areas that need attention." The tool's FAQ section even includes a dedicated entry, "What is a good cost per hire benchmark?", answered with the same $4,700 average and the $14,000+ executive threshold [4].

The guide behind the calculator in [2] and [6] takes a similar approach but leans harder on caution rather than a single comparison figure. It states plainly that "A good cost per hire is not simply a low one. A lower number can look efficient while hiding poor outcomes," and instructs readers to track cost per hire "alongside: Time to hire, Offer acceptance rate, New hire retention, Quality of hire" rather than judging the raw output in isolation [2][6]. It also demonstrates why comparing directly to a headline average is misleading, walking through a worked example where a 40-person company's calculated cost per hire ($1,875) sits far below the cited SHRM average ($5,475), concluding "That's well below the SHRM average, and it should be... The point isn't to hit a benchmark. It's to know your own number well enough to notice when it moves" [2][6].

The guide in [3] provides the most granular interpretive scaffolding of the sources gathered. Beyond a single average, it publishes benchmark tables segmented by company size (small businesses under 100 employees at $3,500–$5,500; mid-market at $2,500–$4,500; enterprise at $1,500–$3,500) and by role type (hourly/frontline at $1,000–$2,500 up through executive/VP-and-above at $15,000–$50,000+), explicitly framing the point of these breakdowns: "the SHRM benchmark places average US cost per hire at approximately $4,700. But here's what that number doesn't tell you: whether $4,700 is good or bad depends entirely on your role mix, company size, and industry" [3].

The Juicebox-linked guide in [5] goes furthest in resisting a single "good" comparison figure. Its benchmarks section states that "there's no specific 'good' target to aim for. What matters is tracking CPH consistently within your own context, so you can spot trends, compare across role types, and make a defensible case for recruiting budget," while still citing SHRM's $4,425–$4,800 range and noting executive roles "often exceed $14,000" as a directional reference point [5]. It recommends segmenting the metric by role level, department, and sourcing channel before drawing any conclusion about whether a number is high or low.

The Pin-linked article in [1] follows the same pattern at greater length, publishing separate benchmark tables by role seniority, by industry, and by company size, all built around the same SHRM 2025 figures ($5,475 non-executive, $35,879 executive) as the anchor comparison point [1].

Taken together, the gathered information indicates that vendor cost-per-hire tools do not present the formula and result as an isolated, context-free number. They consistently attach it to a stated benchmark (most commonly the SHRM figure, cited variously as $4,700, $4,425–$4,800, or the updated 2025 figure of $5,475/$35,879 depending on the source's publication date), and the more developed guides extend that into explicit ranges by role, industry, and company size, alongside cautionary language that a lower cost per hire does not by itself indicate a "good" outcome. I cannot confirm from the gathered information whether hireTruffle's own calculator page specifically includes this benchmark context, since none of the excerpts are uniquely attributable to hireTruffle by name (source [1] only mentions "Truffle" as a cited research source for a separate statistic, not as the calculator being described) — that would need to be verified directly against hireTruffle's site.

But many employers estimate the total cost to hire a new employee can be three to four times the position's salary, according to Edie Goldberg, founder of the Menlo Park, Calif.-based talent management and development company E.L. Goldberg & Associates. That means if you're hiring for a job that pays $60,000, you may spend $180,000 or more to fill that role. "Of those costs, I would say 30 percent to 40 percent are hard costs, and the other 60 percent are soft costs," said Goldberg, who is also the SHRM Foundation chair-elect and co-author of the book The Inside Gig (LifeTree, 2020). Soft costs include the time departmental leaders and managers invest in supporting the HR-specific roles of the hiring process. When these are added to the hard costs, the price of recruiting skyrockets. "When all of these professionals are meeting with potential candidates, screening applications, scheduling a few rounds of interviews and making final decisions, it takes away time from accomplishing organizational goals/outcomes,
[1]: which then certainly ties to ROI [return on investment]," said Ankit Shah, supervisor of talent development at Columbus State Community College in Ohio. Here's a look at other indirect costs to consider. The Impact on Productivity Goldberg said most people don't consider the expense of losing somebody on a team. "It disrupts the flow of how things get done. Teams can become unmoored," she said. Organization network analysis looks at ties between different employees. Some staff members are "brokers" of information across different teams or subfunctions in organizations. Losing one of those individuals can interrupt information flows crucial to getting the work done. Goldberg suggests implementing stay interviews. Retaining employees is directly tied to reducing recruitment costs. In addition, these types of conversations can shed light on an individual's concerns that factor in deciding to stay or leave. For example, many parents and caregivers are concerned about going back to the office because they are afraid of bringing the COVID-19 virus home. Other workers may see positions similar to theirs at other companies that pay higher salaries or offer better benefits. Scheduling time
[1]: to talk with employees about their most pressing concerns can reveal solutions to help them stay rather than leave. The Emotional Toll More demands for higher compensation, time off, flexible work schedules and perks are taking a financial toll on organizations, according to Sharon DeLay, SHRM-SCP, founder of GO-HR, a full-service consulting firm in Columbus, Ohio. All of this creates mental exhaustion and fatigue for hiring teams. "The mental and emotional toll of all the ghosting, demands, etc., aren't sustainable and likely causes them to lose focus on other duties," she said. The Cost of Competition There's also a price for what DeLay calls lost candidates. Most smaller businesses are not prepared to move quickly. So they must fight harder to recruit candidates, and then if they don't offer the job fast enough, the candidates are snapped up by another employer. Losing a great candidate for the role midway through the interview process due to external competition also has financial ramifications. "Recruiters and HR people, especially in smaller companies, need to be empowered so they can be quick," she said. Goldberg predicts that 2022 is going to be the year of the employee exp

What Is Cost Per Hire and How Do You Calculate It? Cost per hire (CPH) measures the total amount your company spends to fill one open position. SHRM and the American National Standards Institute formalized the CPH formula in 2012 via the ANSI/SHRM 06001.2012 standard, giving teams a shared methodology for comparing against industry hiring benchmarks. Widely adopted since 2012, this formula remains the universal benchmark for comparing CPH across organizations of different sizes, industries, and hiring volumes. Calculating it follows a single formula, standardized by SHRM and the American National Standards Institute in 2012: Cost Per Hire = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) / Total Number of Hires Simple on paper. message.content:
Citation practices vary sharply across these sources, and the variation itself is the story.

At the careful end, the interview-cost-calculator guide [8] treats sourcing as its whole point: it lays out a table naming each SHRM edition, its publication date, and the resulting figure — Human Capital Benchmarking Report (fiscal year 2015, published 8 August 2016) for $4,129; SHRM's "The Real Costs of Recruitment" (11 April 2022) for the "nearly $4,700" figure; and the 2025 SHRM Benchmarking Report (released 15 October 2025) for $5,475 non-executive and $35,879 executive. It even states the figures were "re-verified against SHRM on 2026-07-01." That's the only source among these that lets a reader tell, at a glance, which SHRM number they're looking at and when it was collected.

The Pin/Truffle-style calculator guide [2, 7] does something similar but folds it into running prose rather than a table: it names "SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report" as the source for both the $5,475 non-executive figure and the $35,879 executive figure (noting the latter is up 21% from 2022), and it explicitly flags the older number — "the SHRM average cost per hire of $4,700 from older benchmarking resources reflects a prior SHRM benchmarking cycle." So this vendor actively distinguishes current from superseded data rather than blending them.

SHRM's own original reporting [1, 5, 6, 9, 15] anchors its figures to survey mechanics rather than just a headline number — the $4,129 figure, for instance, comes with the collection window (February-April), the fiscal year it reflects (2015), and the sample size (2,048 SHRM members) [5, 9, 15]. The "nearly $4,700" SHRM.org piece [1, 6] identifies itself as "new benchmarking data" tied to the SHRM Talent Conference & Expo 2022, though within that excerpt it doesn't spell out the report's formal name or exact publication date the way [8] does.

Other vendor guides are looser, and this is where an outdated-figure problem shows up. One SMB-focused guide [3] states that "SHRM reports that average cost per hire has jumped from $4,129 in 2019 to $4,700 in 2023 — a 14% increase." That dating doesn't match what the primary sources show: $4,129 traces to fiscal year 2015 data [5, 9, 15], and $4,700 traces to an April 2022 SHRM article [8], not 2019 and 2023 respectively. The same guide also cites an executive average of "$28,329" with no report name, edition, or date attached at all. Because this guide never mentions SHRM's 2025 update to $5,475/$35,879, it presents a 2022-vintage (mislabeled as 2023) figure as the current picture, with no signal to the reader that a newer benchmark exists.

A clearer case of implying currency for a stale figure appears in the Teamed-style guide [4, 10]. Its "Quick Facts" section opens by citing "$5,475 for nonexecutive roles according to SHRM's 2025 benchmark" and separately notes "$35,879 average for executives" from the same 2025 data. But later in the same document, it states flatly: "The SHRM benchmark places average US cost per hire at approximately $4,700" — with no edition, no year, and no acknowledgment that this is the superseded figure it already cited a newer number for elsewhere. Read in isolation, that later sentence reads as if $4,700 were still "the" current SHRM benchmark, even though the same guide has already established that SHRM updated it to $5,475. That internal inconsistency, an undated figure sitting alongside an explicitly dated newer one in the same piece, is the clearest example in this set of a vendor resource using an older number in a way that implies it's current.

So the overall pattern: rigor ranges from a fully dated, edition-labeled table [8], through prose that names the specific report and flags supersession [2, 7], down to guides that either mis-date their SHRM citation [3] or drop the date/edition entirely for a figure that has since been revised [4, 10]. None of the gathered sources shows an hireTruffle-branded calculator tool itself presenting a bare, undated benchmark number in its own interface (the Truffle citation here [2, 7] is used only as a source for a separate underestimation statistic, with the CPH benchmark itself attributed to SHRM's 2025 report), so I can't confirm or rule out that specific tool's on-page citation behavior from what's gathered here.

What Is Cost Per Hire and How Do You Calculate It? Cost per hire (CPH) measures the total amount your company spends to fill one open position. SHRM and the American National Standards Institute formalized the CPH formula in 2012 via the ANSI/SHRM 06001.2012 standard, giving teams a shared methodology for comparing against industry hiring benchmarks. Widely adopted since 2012, this formula remains the universal benchmark for comparing CPH across organizations of different sizes, industries, and hiring volumes. Calculating it follows a single formula, standardized by SHRM and the American National Standards Institute in 2012: Cost Per Hire = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) / Total Number of Hires Simple on paper. Ask them what a single hire actually costs the business, and you'll get a pause, a rough estimate, or a confession that nobody's tracking it properly. That gap isn't just an analytics problem. It's a budget problem. Without knowing your cost per hire, you can't justify recruiting investment to Finance, diagnose where your process leaks money, or make the case for better tooling. You're flying blind on one of your largest controllable expenses. Here's how to calculate cost per hire using the SHRM-standard formula, what your number actually means compared to benchmarks, and what to do if it's higher than it should be. Quick Facts: Cost Per Hire Benchmarks and Data Points The average cost per hire in the US is approximately $5,475 for nonexecutive roles according to SHRM's 2025 benchmark, though international teams should treat this as directional rather than directly comparable due to wage and vendor-price differences across markets. [12]: r mixed hiring plans, with role mix moving the figure materially even when the process remains unchanged. Executive hiring at VP level and above commonly benchmarks at $15,000 to $50,000+ when search fees, assessments, and multi-stakeholder time are included, with SHRM's 2025 data showing $35,879 average for executives. Recruiting agency fees for permanent placements commonly range from 15% to 25% of first-year base salary, making agency usage one of the largest single drivers of cost per hire. Employee referral bonuses in mid-market companies commonly land between $500 and $5,000 per successful hire, and should be counted as external recruiting cost. What Is Cost Per Hire? The SHRM-Standard Definition Cost per hire is the total sum of internal and external recruiting costs divided by the number of hires in a given period. The formula is straightforward: (Internal Recruiting Costs + External Recruiting Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires. Internal costs include everything your organi
[12]: sation pays internally to make a hire happen. Think recruiter salaries allocated by time spent, hiring manager interview hours, HR coordination time, and prorated recruiting technology subscriptions. External costs are third-party invoiceable expenses: job board spend, agency fees, background checks, assessments, and referral bonuses. The SHRM benchmark places average US cost per hire at approximately $4,700. But here's what that number doesn't tell you: whether $4,700 is good or bad depends entirely on your role mix, company size, and industry. The same salary benchmarking principles that guide compensation decisions also affect recruiting cost expectations. A company hiring mostly junior roles at $4,700 per hire is overspending. An enterprise hiring executives at that rate is getting a bargain. What cost per hire is NOT: it doesn't include post-hire costs like training beyond initial onboarding, productivity ramp time, or ongoing employment costs. Those belong to different metrics like cost-of-vacancy and time-to-productivity. What Should You Include in Your Cost Per Hire Calculation? The formula is simple. Internal costs (time-based, must be allocated): Recruiter salary allocation is calculated by multiplying their annual compensation by the percentage of time spent on hiring. If a recruiter earns $80,000 per year and spends 60% of their time on active recruiting, allocate $48,000 to your cost per hire pool, then divide by annual hires. Hiring manager interview time uses their hourly rate multiplied by hours spent interviewing candidates, though managers typically spend only 13% of their total time on hiring and onboarding tasks. HR admin and coordination time follows the same calculation. ATS and recruiting software subscriptions should be prorated annually and divided across hires. External costs (invoice-based, sum directly): Job board postings on platforms like Indeed and LinkedIn typically range from $200 to $1,500 per posting. Recruiting agency and staffing fees run 15-25% of first-year salary. Background checks and assessm
[12]: ent tools cost $30 to $200 per candidate screened. Employee referral bonuses range from $500 to $5,000 per successful hire. Relocation assistance, when applicable, can add $5,000 to $20,000+ per hire. Conditional inclusions: Employer branding and careers page spend should be prorated annually and amortised across total hires. Onboarding materials and software are optional depending on your organisation's cost allocation philosophy. Training beyond Day 1 belongs in your L&D budget, not cost per hire. How Do You Calculate Cost Per Hire Step by Step? Here's the process that produces a number Finance can actually audit and reproduce each period. 1. Define your time period. Choose a consistent window: monthly, quarterly, or annually. Annual is most reliable for smoothing seasonal variance, but quarterly tracking lets you course-correct faster. Monthly tracking makes sense only during high-volume hiring pushes or when testing new sourcing channels. 2. Tally all internal costs. List every internal stakeholder involved in recruiting. Multiply their hourly rate by hours spent. Include recruiter time, hiring manager interviews, HR coordination, and any internal tools prorated per hire. Don't
[12]: forget to include the prorated cost of your ATS subscription. 3. Tally all external costs. Based on the available sources, the ANSI/SHRM cost-per-hire standard and the benchmark dollar figures come from two distinct, separately published sources — and the gathered material supports that distinction clearly.

The standard itself — ANSI/SHRM 06001-2012, developed jointly by the Society for Human Resource Management and the American National Standards Institute through a voluntary consensus standards development process [6] — defines only the calculation methodology. Its content is the formula and the cost taxonomy: Cost Per Hire = (Total External Costs + Total Internal Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires, along with detailed definitions of what belongs in the internal-cost bucket (recruiter salaries and benefits, hiring manager interview time, referral payouts, ATS and recruiting technology, administrative overhead) and the external-cost bucket (agency and search-firm fees, job board postings, background checks, assessments, travel and relocation) [4][5][9][12]. One source describes the document itself as a roughly 50-page American National Standard whose entire substantive content is that single quotient formula, written to get HR and Finance functions to agree on a shared definition — it contains no discussion of what a "normal" or "high" number looks like [8]. A related standards fragment also references the standard defining cost per hire in relation to comparing total hiring cost against new hires' first-year compensation, again framed as a definitional/methodological point rather than a benchmark [3].

Nowhere in the material describing the standard's content ([3], [6], [8], and the methodology sections of [4], [9], [12]) is there any mention of the standard itself publishing threshold values, target ranges, or "good/bad" classifications. Multiple sources make this gap explicit: one notes that "there's no specific 'good' target to aim for" within the formula itself, and that SHRM's average-cost figures are reported separately and "vary by year and methodology" [5]. Another states plainly that the SHRM benchmark of roughly $4,700 "doesn't tell you... whether $4,700 is good or bad depends entirely on your role mix, company size, and industry" — treating interpretation as something added on top of the standard's raw formula, not part of it [12].

The dollar benchmarks vendors cite — $4,700, $4,425–$4,800, $5,475 for non-executive roles, and $35,879 for executive roles — are consistently attributed not to the ANSI/SHRM standard document but to separate, periodically updated SHRM survey publications: SHRM's Human Capital Benchmarking Report and its 2025 Benchmarking Report specifically [2][9][12][13]. These are described as distinct data-collection efforts that apply the standard's formula across surveyed organizations and then publish aggregate results, with figures that shift from cycle to cycle (the $4,700 figure is explicitly identified as coming from "a prior SHRM benchmarking cycle," superseded by the $5,475 figure in the 2025 report) [2][9][13]. One source's audit-framework treatment of cost per hire reinforces this separation structurally, listing "Adopt the SHRM/ANSI standard cost-per-hire formula as the calculation baseline" as one action item and, as a distinct later action item, "Benchmark cost per hire against published industry standards and peer data... SHRM's annual Human Capital Benchmarking Report, CIPD's Resourcing and Talent Planning Survey, and industry-specific benchmarks from consultancies such as Bersin, PwC Saratoga, or Mercer" [4] — treating formula-adoption and benchmarking against survey data as two separate steps rather than one.

In short: the standard document defines the calculation methodology and cost categorization only, with no published "good/bad" thresholds, while the specific dollar benchmarks vendors and calculators cite come entirely from separate SHRM benchmarking survey reports (and third-party analyses of them, such as ScoutLogic's and TimeClick's role- and industry-level breakdowns cited in [2]/[9]/[13]) that apply the standard's formula to surveyed data and publish results independently of the standard itself.

Your persona besides being a Wikipedia writer: Basic fact writer: Basic fact writer focusing on broadly covering the basic facts about the topic.

Conversation history:
You: When you look at calculators like hireTruffle's, what specific line items or input fields do they typically ask users to fill in, and how are those grouped (e.g., advertising spend, agency fees, internal recruiter time, onboarding costs)?
Expert: Calculators of this type consistently organize their input fields around the two categories defined by the ANSI/SHRM standard formula, internal recruitment costs and external recruitment costs, though the granularity and grouping labels vary by vendor.
**A representative example: the ANSI/SHRM-standard calculator**
One calculator built explicitly on the ANSI/SHRM formula groups its fields into four sections :
1. **General Settings** — currency (from 15 global options), reporting period (Annual, Semi-Annual, Quarterly, or Monthly, which determines how salary figures are prorated), and Total Hires, which serves as the divisor in the final formula.
2. **Internal Recruitment Costs** — HR/Recruiting Staff Salaries (annual compensation for in-house recruiting personnel, automatically prorated to the selected reporting period), Employee Referral Awards (bonuses paid to employees for successful referrals), Interview Expenses (interviewer time and materials), and Signing Bonuses.
3. **External Recruitment Costs** — Job Board/Advertising Fees (spending on job postings and paid channels), Recruitment Agency Fees, ATS/Technology Costs (subscription and licensing fees for applicant tracking systems), and Background Checks/Drug Testing.
4. **Advanced Options** — Relocation Fees, Candidate Travel Expenses, Job Fairs/Recruiting Events, and Average First-Year Salary, the last of which is optional and only feeds a secondary output (the Recruiting Cost Ratio) rather than the core cost-per-hire number itself .
The output layer built on these inputs includes the internal-versus-external cost split as a percentage, and, if the first-year salary field is filled in, the Recruiting Cost Ratio, which expresses total recruitment spend as a percentage of first-year compensation .
**How other vendor tools vary the grouping**
Other calculators follow the same internal/external skeleton but differ in how many line items they expose and where they draw category boundaries:
- A calculator built for staffing agencies keeps the same two-bucket structure but adds staffing-specific internal items such as prorated recruiter/sourcer salaries, ATS/CRM/video-interviewing subscriptions, and training costs for new recruiting staff, alongside the standard external items (job board fees, background checks, assessments, relocation, third-party vendor fees) .
- A more elaborate calculator splits inputs into three groups rather than two: **Direct costs** (job ads, agency fees, background checks, assessment tools, candidate travel, and ATS cost attributed to the hire), **Indirect costs** (internal recruiter hours, hiring manager hours, interview panel hours, and days the role sits open, each multiplied by an hourly rate or daily cost), and **Post-hire costs** (onboarding program cost, training during ramp, manager coaching hours, and a productivity-ramp cost tied to months-to-full-productivity) .
- A simpler, real-time version asks only for total external costs and total internal costs, recalculates the split as the user types, and surfaces the internal/external ratio "most teams miss" as its main added value beyond the raw number .
**Where the grouping connects back to methodology**
In every case reviewed, the calculator's input groupings map directly onto the same internal-cost/external-cost split used in the underlying ANSI/SHRM formula and in general cost-per-hire explainer content, so the tool functions as an interactive front end for that formula rather than a standalone input form with its own separate logic . The calculators built by content-marketing or blog-style sources tend to surround the input form with the fuller methodology, definitions of hard versus soft/hidden costs (hiring manager time, productivity loss during vacancy, administrative overhead, ramp-up cost), and benchmark tables, whereas the bare ANSI/SHRM-formula calculator presents the input groups with comparatively less surrounding explanatory content on hidden or indirect costs.

You: Is there a recognized formal standard, such as the ANSI/SHRM cost-per-hire standard, that defines exactly which expenses count as "hard costs" versus "soft costs," and if so, how does that standard recommend allocating soft costs like recruiter and hiring manager time, which don't have a clean invoice the way job-ad spend or agency fees do?
Expert: Yes — there is a recognized formal standard. In 2012, the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) jointly formalized a cost-per-hire methodology as ANSI/SHRM 06001:2012, developed through a voluntary consensus standards development process . One commentator who reviewed the published document independently confirmed it runs to roughly 50 pages, even though the underlying formula it standardizes is a simple quotient: CPH = (External Costs + Internal Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires in a Time Period . The standard defines cost-per-hire itself as "the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires" .
On terminology, it's worth being precise about what the standard itself calls the two buckets. The ANSI/SHRM standard's own vocabulary is internal costs versus external costs, not "hard costs" versus "soft costs." It "explicitly delineates internal vs. external cost components" , describing internal cost factors as "staff, capital, and organizational costs of the recruiting function, including fully loaded recruiting salaries and talent acquisition system costs," and external categories as items like advertising, background checks, campus recruiting, RPO fees, sourcing costs, recruiting technology, agency fees, and travel expenses . The "hard cost / soft cost" framing that appears in the gathered sources comes from practitioner commentary layered on top of that structure — for example, Edie Goldberg, SHRM Foundation chair-elect and co-author of The Inside Gig, estimates that of total hiring spend, "30 percent to 40 percent are hard costs, and the other 60 percent are soft costs," with soft costs described as "the time departmental leaders and managers invest in supporting the HR-specific roles of the hiring process" . In practice this hard/soft split tracks closely with the standard's own external/internal split (external, invoiced spend behaving like "hard costs"; internal, time-based effort behaving like "soft costs"), but the sources gathered here do not show the ANSI/SHRM standard itself using "hard" and "soft" as defined terms.
On how soft, non-invoiced costs like recruiter and hiring-manager time get allocated, the standard and the secondary guidance built on it converge on a time-based allocation method rather than a literal invoice:
- **Recruiter time** is allocated by multiplying the recruiter's compensation by the share of their time spent on active recruiting. One worked example: a recruiter earning $80,000 a year who spends 60% of their time recruiting contributes $48,000 to the cost-per-hire pool, which is then divided across that period's hires .
- **Hiring manager time** is allocated by multiplying an hourly rate by the hours spent interviewing and reviewing candidates . Some organizations extend this same hourly-rate-times-hours logic to any interviewer, not just the hiring manager, assigning a monetary value to the hours "team interviewers spend on recruiting" .
- **HR admin/coordination time** follows the same hours-times-rate calculation as recruiter and manager time .
- Recruiter and interviewer training, while not tied to any single hire, is treated as an internal cost that "can be allocated across hires as part of internal recruiting investment" rather than assigned to one requisition .

First, the standard does not require the same precision for these estimated, time-based figures as for invoiced spend: "the SHRM standard calls for high data quality, not a penny-by-penny reconciliation like financial reporting," and guidance built on it explicitly says that where inputs like recruiter salary allocation are estimates, "that's normal," while agency invoices remain exact . **Applicant tracking system (ATS) and talent acquisition software vendors.** iCIMS, an ATS and talent acquisition platform, builds cost-per-hire tracking directly into its product: its "Cost-Per-Hire Report" automatically calculates and segments CPH, and its Expense Tracking feature lets users attach internal and external costs to a job profile. iCIMS also publishes the calculation methodology on its own "Hiring Blog," walking through a full worked example with department- and role-level segmentation . A second, unnamed calculator in the gathered material is explicitly framed around ATS adoption. It asks users to weigh application volume, staff hours, HR salaries, and advertising and agency fees, then states the tool "will determine how much you could be saving by implementing an ATS," making the calculator a lead-in to an ATS sales pitch rather than a neutral benchmarking tool .
**Recruitment process outsourcing (RPO) and professional search firms.** Hire Velocity describes itself as "a Full-Service Talent Acquisition and Professional Search Firm" offering RPO, executive-level professional search, talent advisory (employer branding), and managed service provider (MSP) recruiting management. Its free calculator sits inside marketing content that walks from "your snapshot" of direct and indirect costs straight into client testimonials and a pitch to reduce cost-per-hire by outsourcing to Hire Velocity .
**Broader HR/workforce-management software platforms.** Connecteam, described as "the platform for managing your team," offers a free Cost per Hire Calculator as one utility inside a wider suite covering job posting, applicant tracking, onboarding with e-signatures, and compliance document storage. Its CPH tool is presented as simple input-and-calculate, distinguishing only internal costs (HR salaries, referral awards, signing bonuses, interview costs) from external costs (job board fees, ATS fees, background checks, drug testing) .
**Global employment / Employer of Record (EOR) providers.** Teamed publishes cost-per-hire guidance aimed at mid-market companies managing international teams, and it explicitly ties the CPH formula to the complications of global hiring, noting that "the costs that sit inside recruiting CPH versus ongoing employment cost change depending on whether you're using contractors, EOR, or owned entities" .
**Labor-rights and ethical-recruitment organizations.** Initiative Verité is a notable outlier among these publishers: rather than an HR/recruiting vendor, it is a labor-rights-oriented body whose Recruitment Cost Calculator (RCC) is designed to help companies, suppliers, and labor agents estimate recruitment fees across industries and migration corridors, flag exploitative or illegitimate charges, and progress toward an "Employer Pays" model where workers are not charged recruitment fees. It supplements the calculator with an "Employer Pays Maturity Matrix" for self-assessment and a forthcoming "Performance Dashboard" of industry-wide trends, which positions it closer to a compliance and advocacy tool than a budgeting tool .
**HR standards and benchmarking bodies.** SHRM (Society for Human Resource Management) does not appear in the gathered material as a calculator publisher itself, but nearly every vendor calculator above cites SHRM's ANSI/SHRM standard formula and its benchmark figures (for example, the 2025 Benchmarking Report's average of $5,475 per hire for non-executive roles and $35,879 for executive roles) as the authoritative reference point their own tools calculate against . This makes SHRM function less like a competing calculator vendor and more like the shared methodological anchor that other vendors' tools point back to.
Taken together, the gathered material suggests these calculators are published by four kinds of organizations: ATS/talent-acquisition software vendors (iCIMS, and the unnamed ATS-adoption calculator), RPO/staffing firms (Hire Velocity), general HR/workforce-management platforms (Connecteam), and global-employment or EOR providers (Teamed), plus at least one labor-rights body applying the same cost-accounting logic to a different purpose (Initiative Verité).

Expert: Yes — there is a recognized formal standard. In 2012, the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) jointly formalized a cost-per-hire methodology as ANSI/SHRM 06001:2012, developed through a voluntary consensus standards development process . One commentator who reviewed the published document independently confirmed it runs to roughly 50 pages, even though the underlying formula it standardizes is a simple quotient: CPH = (External Costs + Internal Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires in a Time Period . The standard defines cost-per-hire itself as "the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires" .
On terminology, it's worth being precise about what the standard itself calls the two buckets. The ANSI/SHRM standard's own vocabulary is internal costs versus external costs, not "hard costs" versus "soft costs." It "explicitly delineates internal vs. external cost components" , describing internal cost factors as "staff, capital, and organizational costs of the recruiting function, including fully loaded recruiting salaries and talent acquisition system costs," and external categories as items like advertising, background checks, campus recruiting, RPO fees, sourcing costs, recruiting technology, agency fees, and travel expenses . The "hard cost / soft cost" framing that appears in the gathered sources comes from practitioner commentary layered on top of that structure — for example, Edie Goldberg, SHRM Foundation chair-elect and co-author of The Inside Gig, estimates that of total hiring spend, "30 percent to 40 percent are hard costs, and the other 60 percent are soft costs," with soft costs described as "the time departmental leaders and managers invest in supporting the HR-specific roles of the hiring process" . In practice this hard/soft split tracks closely with the standard's own external/internal split (external, invoiced spend behaving like "hard costs"; internal, time-based effort behaving like "soft costs"), but the sources gathered here do not show the ANSI/SHRM standard itself using "hard" and "soft" as defined terms.
On how soft, non-invoiced costs like recruiter and hiring-manager time get allocated, the standard and the secondary guidance built on it converge on a time-based allocation method rather than a literal invoice:
- **Recruiter time** is allocated by multiplying the recruiter's compensation by the share of their time spent on active recruiting. One worked example: a recruiter earning $80,000 a year who spends 60% of their time recruiting contributes $48,000 to the cost-per-hire pool, which is then divided across that period's hires .
- **Hiring manager time** is allocated by multiplying an hourly rate by the hours spent interviewing and reviewing candidates . Some organizations extend this same hourly-rate-times-hours logic to any interviewer, not just the hiring manager, assigning a monetary value to the hours "team interviewers spend on recruiting" .
- **HR admin/coordination time** follows the same hours-times-rate calculation as recruiter and manager time .
- Recruiter and interviewer training, while not tied to any single hire, is treated as an internal cost that "can be allocated across hires as part of internal recruiting investment" rather than assigned to one requisition .
Two points about data quality bear on this allocation. First, the standard does not require the same precision for these estimated, time-based figures as for invoiced spend: "the SHRM standard calls for high data quality, not a penny-by-penny reconciliation like financial reporting," and guidance built on it explicitly says that where inputs like recruiter salary allocation are estimates, "that's normal," while agency invoices remain exact . Second, because this allocation step depends on organizations actually tracking hours or time-share by role, it's the part of the calculation most often skipped or approximated loosely, which multiple sources cite as the leading reason reported cost-per-hire figures undercount the true cost of hiring .
You: Looking specifically at hireTruffle and comparable vendor cost-per-hire calculators, do their input fields actually separate internal/time-based costs (recruiter hours, hiring manager time) from external/invoiced costs (job ad spend, agency fees) as distinct line items the way the ANSI/SHRM standard does, or do they collapse everything into a small number of simplified fields, and is there any indication of which soft-cost categories get dropped entirely from these tools?
Expert: The vendor calculators show a consistent pattern: they preserve the internal/external structural split that ANSI/SHRM defines, but they simplify what falls inside each bucket, and the soft-cost and opportunity-cost categories are the ones that get dropped or bolted on as "advanced" extras rather than core fields.
**The structural split survives, but with fewer line items than the standard.** The clearest example is the calculator described in source , which is explicitly built on "the ANSI/SHRM standard formula." It keeps Internal Recruitment Costs and External Recruitment Costs as the two top-level buckets, matching the standard's own internal/external division . But within those buckets it reduces to a small, fixed set of fields: internal costs are computed as "Prorated HR Salaries + Employee Referral Awards + Interview Expenses + Signing Bonuses," and external costs as "Job Board Fees + Agency Fees + ATS Costs + Background Checks + Relocation Fees + Travel Expenses + Event Costs" . That is a compact, closed formula, not the open-ended, itemized list the ANSI/SHRM standard document actually enumerates (which covers separate categories like compliance costs, administrative overhead, training and development, sourcing/database subscriptions, and campus recruiting fees as distinct line items ). So the vendor tool keeps the two-bucket architecture but collapses each bucket into a handful of simplified fields, with "advanced options" (relocation, travel, job fair costs, average first-year salary) offered as optional add-ons rather than defaults .
**Time-based costs get folded into a lump sum rather than itemized by role.** The ANSI/SHRM standard and most guides separate hiring manager time from recruiter/sourcer time as distinct internal cost lines, alongside recruiter salaries, referral bonuses, and recruiting technology as their own separate items . In the vendor calculator , this is compressed into a single "Interview Expenses" field plus prorated HR/recruiting staff salaries — there is no separate field for hiring manager time distinct from recruiter time, and no line for recruiting technology/ATS cost sitting in the internal bucket (ATS cost shows up as an external-cost line item instead, whereas fuller breakdowns like and treat recruiting software/ATS as an internal cost). This suggests the internal/time-based side is where vendor tools compress the standard's granularity the most, since accurately costing "hours spent" per stakeholder is harder to input than a lump prorated salary figure.
**Soft costs and opportunity costs are the categories dropped entirely, and this is explicitly documented rather than incidental.** Multiple sources describe this as a known, named gap rather than speculation. Source states directly that "most cost per hire calculators only capture what is apparent to the human eye: Job board fees, recruiter salaries, and agency markups," while the "real budget killers... are hiding in plain sight," listing vacancy costs, overtime/temporary coverage costs, opportunity costs from lost revenue during vacancies, administrative overhead beyond what's tracked, failed-hire/mis-hire costs, benefits and payroll setup time, equipment/workspace costs, ramp-up productivity loss, and background-check coordination time as costs that "rarely make it to CPH calculations" . Source echoes this from a different angle, noting that "even the updated figure only captures what shows up on an invoice" and that hidden costs like "recruiter inefficiencies, longer time-to-fill, wasted job board spend, and the productivity lost while a role sits open" are what most teams still miss . Source quantifies the dropped categories most specifically, citing industry research compiled by Truffle that "38 percent of small and mid-size businesses underestimate their hiring costs" precisely because of "expenses that never make it into the ANSI formula" — explicitly naming vacancy costs (~$500/day, with the median 44-day time-to-fill implying roughly $22,000 in unmeasured vacancy cost before any recruiting fee is even paid), bad-hire costs (30% of first-year salary per the U.S. Department of Labor, ballooning to $30,000–$150,000+ per the Toggl Hire 2025 Report once indirect effects are counted), and the opportunity cost of recruiter time spent on administrative tasks rather than higher-value work .
**The ANSI/SHRM standard itself acknowledges this limitation rather than treating it as a calculator flaw.** Source notes that "the SHRM/ANSI standard is clear that cost per hire does not fully describe recruiting effectiveness on its own and does not account for factors like time to fill, quality of hire, or hiring manager and candidate satisfaction" — meaning the standard was never designed to capture soft/opportunity costs, and vendor calculators that stick to the formula are being faithful to that scope rather than cutting corners against it .
**What this means for connecting a calculator to pillar content:** none of the gathered sources show a calculator UI itself explaining hard-vs-soft cost distinctions, benchmarks, or usage guidance inline — that context appears instead in surrounding article content that frames the calculator (e.g., , , and all pair a calculator or calculator mention with an extended explainer on hidden costs, benchmarks by role/industry, and how to interpret the number against quality-of-hire). So the pattern across these examples is: the calculator itself outputs a bare CPH figure and sometimes an internal/external split percentage , while the pillar-content explanation of hard vs. soft costs, ANSI/SHRM methodology, and "how to use this number" responsibly lives in the surrounding guide, not as an inline feature of the tool.

Topic you want to write: How do existing cost-per-hire calculators from HR/recruiting vendors (e.g., hireTruffle and similar tools) present their line items — do they stand alone as isolated tools, or do any connect their inputs back to a broader cost-per-hire methodology or pillar content explaining hard costs vs soft costs, benchmarks, and how the number should be used?

Your persona besides being a Wikipedia writer: HR-tech vendor landscape editor: Catalogues cost-per-hire calculators from tools like hireTruffle and comparable ATS/recruiting platforms, documenting what inputs each one asks for, how results are displayed, and whether the tool is offered as a standalone widget or embedded within a larger content/product ecosystem.

Conversation history:
You: Could you name some of the most prominent cost-per-hire calculators currently offered by HR/recruiting vendors — beyond hireTruffle — and briefly describe what kind of company (ATS platform, staffing firm, HR consultancy, etc.) tends to publish these tools?
Expert: Beyond hireTruffle, several organizations publish their own cost-per-hire calculators, and the sources gathered here show they fall into a few distinct publisher types.
**Applicant tracking system (ATS) and talent acquisition software vendors.** iCIMS, an ATS and talent acquisition platform, builds cost-per-hire tracking directly into its product: its "Cost-Per-Hire Report" automatically calculates and segments CPH, and its Expense Tracking feature lets users attach internal and external costs to a job profile. iCIMS also publishes the calculation methodology on its own "Hiring Blog," walking through a full worked example with department- and role-level segmentation . A second, unnamed calculator in the gathered material is explicitly framed around ATS adoption. It asks users to weigh application volume, staff hours, HR salaries, and advertising and agency fees, then states the tool "will determine how much you could be saving by implementing an ATS," making the calculator a lead-in to an ATS sales pitch rather than a neutral benchmarking tool .
**Recruitment process outsourcing (RPO) and professional search firms.** Hire Velocity describes itself as "a Full-Service Talent Acquisition and Professional Search Firm" offering RPO, executive-level professional search, talent advisory (employer branding), and managed service provider (MSP) recruiting management. Its free calculator sits inside marketing content that walks from "your snapshot" of direct and indirect costs straight into client testimonials and a pitch to reduce cost-per-hire by outsourcing to Hire Velocity .
**Broader HR/workforce-management software platforms.** Connecteam, described as "the platform for managing your team," offers a free Cost per Hire Calculator as one utility inside a wider suite covering job posting, applicant tracking, onboarding with e-signatures, and compliance document storage. Its CPH tool is presented as simple input-and-calculate, distinguishing only internal costs (HR salaries, referral awards, signing bonuses, interview costs) from external costs (job board fees, ATS fees, background checks, drug testing) .
**Global employment / Employer of Record (EOR) providers.** Teamed publishes cost-per-hire guidance aimed at mid-market companies managing international teams, and it explicitly ties the CPH formula to the complications of global hiring, noting that "the costs that sit inside recruiting CPH versus ongoing employment cost change depending on whether you're using contractors, EOR, or owned entities" .
**Labor-rights and ethical-recruitment organizations.** Initiative Verité is a notable outlier among these publishers: rather than an HR/recruiting vendor, it is a labor-rights-oriented body whose Recruitment Cost Calculator (RCC) is designed to help companies, suppliers, and labor agents estimate recruitment fees across industries and migration corridors, flag exploitative or illegitimate charges, and progress toward an "Employer Pays" model where workers are not charged recruitment fees. It supplements the calculator with an "Employer Pays Maturity Matrix" for self-assessment and a forthcoming "Performance Dashboard" of industry-wide trends, which positions it closer to a compliance and advocacy tool than a budgeting tool .
**HR standards and benchmarking bodies.** SHRM (Society for Human Resource Management) does not appear in the gathered material as a calculator publisher itself, but nearly every vendor calculator above cites SHRM's ANSI/SHRM standard formula and its benchmark figures (for example, the 2025 Benchmarking Report's average of $5,475 per hire for non-executive roles and $35,879 for executive roles) as the authoritative reference point their own tools calculate against . This makes SHRM function less like a competing calculator vendor and more like the shared methodological anchor that other vendors' tools point back to.
Taken together, the gathered material suggests these calculators are published by four kinds of organizations: ATS/talent-acquisition software vendors (iCIMS, and the unnamed ATS-adoption calculator), RPO/staffing firms (Hire Velocity), general HR/workforce-management platforms (Connecteam), and global-employment or EOR providers (Teamed), plus at least one labor-rights body applying the same cost-accounting logic to a different purpose (Initiative Verité).
You: Looking specifically at the input fields these calculators collect, do most of them separate "hard costs" (agency fees, job board spend, background checks) from "soft costs" (recruiter/HR staff time, hiring manager hours, referral bonuses), or do they lump everything into one undifferentiated total? And when the calculation is done, do they show a single output number, or a line-item breakdown the user can compare against a benchmark?
Expert: Across the calculators and guides reviewed, none present their inputs as one undifferentiated total, but few use the literal labels "hard costs" and "soft costs." Instead, nearly all of them organize inputs around the ANSI/SHRM standard's own split of internal versus external recruiting costs , and that split lines up closely with the hard/soft distinction you're describing, even though the vocabulary differs.
**Internal/external as the de facto hard/soft split.** In the ANSI/SHRM framing used by most of these tools, "internal costs" cover recruiter and HR staff salaries, hiring manager interview time, referral bonuses, signing bonuses, and internal recruiting technology , which is essentially the labor-and-time category (your "soft costs"). "External costs" cover job board and advertising fees, agency fees, background checks and drug testing, ATS/technology subscriptions, relocation, candidate travel, and event costs , which is the invoiced, vendor-facing category (your "hard costs"). The Connecteam calculator asks users to enter these as two separate groups explicitly: "Add Internal Costs by entering HR salaries, referral awards, signing bonuses, and interview costs" and then "Include External Costs by entering job board fees, ATS fees, background checks, drug testing, and other external fees" . The calculator built on the ANSI/SHRM formula goes further, prorating HR/recruiting salaries by reporting period as an internal line, and separately summing job board fees, agency fees, ATS costs, background checks, relocation, travel, and event costs as external lines, then computing an internal-to-external percentage split as its own output .
**One tool uses "direct/indirect" language instead, and it doesn't map cleanly.** The Hire Velocity calculator is the one source that uses labels resembling hard/soft costs directly, calling them "Direct Costs" (job advertising, background checks, recruiter fees, onboarding expenses, described as "visible, often tangible... relatively easy to measure and control") and "Indirect Costs" (lost productivity, knowledge gaps left by departing employees, time spent re-engaging candidates, and disruption to teams while positions stay unfilled, described as "hidden costs that can be harder to calculate") . This is a different cut than the internal/external split used elsewhere: Hire Velocity's "indirect" bucket is about opportunity cost and productivity loss rather than staff time spent on recruiting itself, so the vocabulary is not standardized across vendors even where the underlying idea (visible vendor spend vs. harder-to-see costs) is similar.
**One older, simpler tool doesn't categorize at all.** The iCIMS-style basic calculator referenced in one source lists inputs like application volume, staff hours spent on recruiting, HR staff salaries, job posting/agency fees, and new hire volume without presenting them as two labeled cost categories in the interface itself, and it's oriented toward showing potential savings from adopting an ATS rather than a cost breakdown . This is the closest thing among the sources to a lumped, single-purpose tool rather than a categorized CPH breakdown.
**Output: single number plus a breakdown is the norm, not single number alone.** Every calculator with enough detail in the sources produces more than a lone total. The ANSI/SHRM-based calculator outputs the CPH figure itself, then an internal-percentage/external-percentage split, an optional Recruiting Cost Ratio (total recruitment cost as a percentage of average first-year salary), and a worked example table breaking costs down by category and amount (HR salaries, referral bonuses, interview expenses, job board/advertising, ATS fees, background checks, agency fees) . Connecteam advertises that clicking "Calculate" produces "a detailed breakdown of your total cost per hire," not just one figure . The SimpleTexting calculator "updates as you type" and "shows the external versus internal split most teams miss," in addition to giving "a real number to weigh against what a mis-hire in that seat would actually cost you" . Hire Velocity's results page shows a "Cost Per Hire" figure alongside a "Potential Per Hire Savings" estimate and a stated direct/indirect breakdown, though the underlying text is lighter on a granular line-item table than the ANSI/SHRM-based tool .
**Benchmarking is attached to most of these, usually via the surrounding content rather than the widget alone.** The SimpleTexting guide frames its calculator inside an article citing SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report ($5,475 average for non-executive roles, $35,879 for executive roles) and explicitly tells readers to compare their number against it, while cautioning that "a cheaper hire isn't automatically a better one," citing CareerBuilder's roughly $17,000 average cost of a bad hire . The ANSI/SHRM-based calculator's page cites the older $4,700 SHRM average alongside sector notes (healthcare and technology skew higher, retail and hospitality skew lower) as reference points for interpreting a user's result . Hire Velocity's page markets "Benchmarking against industry averages" as one of the calculator's stated benefits . The iCIMS blog, which is more of a methodology article than a bare calculator, goes furthest on this front: it walks through a full worked example (own CPH of $4,625 against a SHRM 2022 mean of $4,700, and roughly $6,500 for technical/communications companies specifically) and then segments cost per hire further by department, role, and recruitment channel, explicitly stating that "analyzing your cost-per-hire data in isolation doesn't provide much insight" and that it needs to be broken down by demographics and data points to identify inefficiencies .
**On whether these stand alone or connect to a broader methodology.** Based on the gathered material, none of the calculators function as an isolated, context-free widget. Each one sits inside an article or guide that explains the ANSI/SHRM formula, defines what counts as internal versus external cost, and supplies benchmark figures for comparison . The degree of connection varies: the ANSI/SHRM-based tool and the iCIMS guide tie the calculator most tightly to a documented standard and to segmented analysis, while the older, simpler tool is closer to a standalone lead-generation widget with minimal categorization or benchmarking context. I cannot fully characterize Dora Domosi's "Navigating Recruitment Costs" piece , since the gathered excerpt for that source contains only a title and byline with no further content.

Expert: The ANSI/SHRM cost-per-hire standard, formally designated ANSI/SHRM 06001:2012, is a standardized methodology for calculating the average cost an organization spends to fill an open position . It was developed through a formal collaboration between the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), with SHRM developing the standard and ANSI approving it in 2012 . Under this standard, the metric is officially termed "Cost-per-Hire, Internal" (CPHI), and its formula definition is designed to measure the costs associated with sourcing, recruiting, and staffing a position .

One CPH guide states this explicitly as a rule to follow rather than a problem to solve: "Keep all three tied to the same time window," referring to internal costs, external costs, and hire count, with no provision for carrying a cost forward or back to the period in which its associated hire actually closes .
The one place a timing adjustment appears in the CPH formula is HR/recruiting salary proration, where an annual salary figure is divided by a period divisor (1 for annual, 2 for semi-annual, 4 for quarterly, or 12 for monthly) to fit the chosen reporting window . This is a period-length conversion, not a cost-to-unit matching. It answers "how much of this annual salary belongs in a quarter," not "which specific hire did this recruiter's time produce." A recruiter's fully loaded compensation and a job board's advertising fee are treated as period costs, counted in whichever calendar window they fall into, regardless of whether the requisition they supported actually converts into a filled seat in that same window or a later one .
This stands in contrast to how the matching principle and amortization actually work in accounting, per the gathered material. The matching principle requires that an expense be recognized in the same period as the revenue it helped generate, even when cash or billing timing falls elsewhere, such as recording a December bonus as a December expense even though it is paid in January, or deferring inventory cost until the period the related sale occurs rather than the period the inventory was purchased . Amortization and depreciation apply the same logic to costs that span many periods, spreading an asset's cost over its useful life, or a multi-year contract's cost over the months it covers, so the expense recognized in any given period lines up with the benefit or output that period actually received . None of the CPH sources describe an equivalent step, such as deferring a recruiter's salary cost into the period a requisition actually closes, or amortizing a long, multi-quarter search across the eventual hire it produces.
The practical effect shows up in how the CPH literature itself flags the metric's blind spots, even without naming them in matching-principle terms. One guide notes that standard CPH tracking misses vacancy costs, the ongoing productivity loss for every day a role sits open, precisely because the ANSI formula only counts costs and hires that fall inside the fixed window, not a cost's downstream effect on a hire that lands in a different window . That same source flags that recruiter time spent sourcing for a role that has not yet closed does not appear anywhere in the official CPH number, describing it as one of several "hidden costs" that "never make it into the ANSI formula," which is consistent with a pooled, period-bound calculation rather than a cost-to-hire matched one . The historical benchmark figures reinforce the same period-bound framing: SHRM's $4,129 average is explicitly tied to fiscal year 2015 data collected in a specific window, and is presented as a snapshot for that period rather than a trailing or amortized figure .
So, within the gathered information, CPH practice as codified in ANSI/SHRM 06001.2012 pools all recruiting costs and all hires within a fixed calendar window, and prorates only for period length, without a matching-principle or amortization step that would attribute a given period's spend to the later period in which the resulting hire is actually completed . I cannot find, in the material gathered, any explicit discussion in the CPH literature itself of the timing-mismatch problem framed in accounting terms, so any statement that the standard has considered and rejected such an approach would go beyond what these sources support.
